sens: Persist in an action, remain in the process of doing something.
Pursue without interruption for a certain duration.
G1300.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of continuing, of persisting in what one is doing. It is to remain engaged in an ongoing activity. In Acts 27:33, Paul urges the sailors to continue taking food: they have not eaten for a long time, and he encourages them to persevere in this vital act.

2. This meaning emphasizes duration, the absence of interruption: one does not stop, one maintains the same action. The word is based on the idea of traversing time ("dia-" = through) and accomplishing ("-téléō"). That is why one can also say "to accomplish to the end": to continue is to go to the end without failing.
G1300.origine: The word is formed from two Greek roots: "dia-" (through, during) and "téléō" (to accomplish, to bring to completion, to finish). This composition suggests the idea of traversing a period or an action while bringing it to completion. In Hebrew, this verb sometimes translates "hayah" (to be, to remain) when it concerns persisting in a state or action (Deuteronomy 9:7), or "kalah" (to finish, to cease), but with the opposite meaning: to continue despite everything. It is a rich verb, where "to continue" and "to accomplish to the end" are very close.
G1300.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: Acts 27:33. In this account of a storm at sea, Paul urges the 276 passengers of the ship to eat, for they have taken nothing for fourteen days. "Continue," here, takes the meaning of "to persist in" or "to apply oneself to": he encourages them to pursue the act of nourishing themselves. The context shows that the word comes into play at a critical moment, where endurance and obedience to the exhortations of the wise become a matter of survival. It is a verb of courageous and persevering action.
G1300.portee: This verb invites the reader to reflect on perseverance and endurance in faith. The scene of the imminent shipwreck reveals that to continue — to eat, to maintain strength — is to trust in God's direction through His servant. For the Christian, this word reminds us that "to continue" is never trivial: it is to obey, to cling to the life that God gives, to listen to His word even in the midst of the storm.

sens: To carefully preserve something in memory or in one's heart
To attentively observe a rule or prescription to maintain it
To preserve oneself or to stay away from something with vigilance
G1301.detail:
1. To carefully keep means first to preserve something precious, not materially, but in one's heart or mind. This is what Mary does in Luke 2:51, when she "keeps all these things in her heart": she meditates, she retains, she preserves the memory of the wonderful events concerning Jesus, constantly turning them over in her mind.

2. The word can also refer to the vigilant observation of a rule or prohibition. In Acts 15:29, the assembly urges Christians to be on guard "against" certain practices: not to eat meat sacrificed to idols, not to drink blood. It is to keep a line of conduct, to ensure not to deviate from it, to firmly maintain one's moral boundaries.
G1301.origine: The Greek word comes from two parts: "dia" (through, completely) and "tēreō" (to keep, to observe, to protect). This composition reinforces the meaning: it is not a simple safeguard, it is a complete, vigilant, and internal guard. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) used this word to translate the Hebrew "shamar" (to keep, to observe, to protect) and "natzar" (to keep, to preserve), terms that evoke both memory and vigilance.
G1301.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, always in the sense of an internal or vigilant guard. In Luke 2:51, it describes Mary keeping the words and actions of Jesus in her heart—not to forget, but to ruminate, to preserve as a treasure. In Acts 15:29, the same verb expresses the idea of staying away, abstaining: to keep a distance, to observe a rule to remain pure. In both cases, it is an active, conscious guard, motivated by love or piety.
G1301.portee: This word invites the reader to two essential attitudes: first, to contemplate and meditate on the works of God, like Mary, by keeping them alive in one's heart and mind. Secondly, to vigilantly observe the moral principles and limits that God sets, staying away from evil not out of servile fear, but out of love and respect. It is a guard that engages the whole person, heart and conduct.

sens: To assign, to entrust something to someone
To bequeath by will, to establish the clauses of a last will
To conclude, to establish a covenant or treaty with someone
G1303.detail:
1. To dispose of something for the benefit of someone: it is to entrust it, to assign it as a favor or gift. Jesus tells His disciples that He "disposes of the kingdom in their favor," as His Father has done for Him (Luke 22:29)—He gives it to them, He ordains it for them.
2. To dispose of one's goods by will: it is to arrange one's succession, to write the clauses of a last will. The Epistle to the Hebrews explains that a will is only valid if the testator is dead; otherwise, it is "just a worthless act" (Hebrews 9:16-17).
3. To conclude a covenant with someone: it is to establish a treaty or pact. God "made a covenant with our fathers, saying to Abraham" (Acts 3:25), and He "will make a covenant with the house of Israel, putting His laws in their minds" (Hebrews 8:10).
G1303.origine: The verb comes from διά ("through") and τίθημι ("to place, to put"). The basic image is therefore: "to place on both sides" or "to arrange, to organize." In the middle voice (the form used in the New Testament), it primarily means "to dispose, to organize for oneself" or "to give with authority." In ancient Greek, it is used for testing, bequeathing, and concluding treaties. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it mainly translates the Hebrew verb "karath" (to cut), which evokes the solemn act of concluding a covenant by "cutting" sacrificial victims.
G1303.emploi: This verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, almost always in Paul or in the epistles. It never appears in the Gospel itself, but Jesus uses it once in Luke (22:29) to express that He "disposes" of the kingdom for His disciples. The pivotal meaning is "to conclude a covenant": this is how it appears in Acts 3:25 (the covenant with Abraham) and three times in the Epistle to the Hebrews (8:10, 10:16) for the new covenant announced by Jeremiah. Hebrews 9:16-17 uses the word in the sense of "to test, to bequeath"—to justify that Christ had to die before the new covenant took effect. The context changes the meaning: with a complement "covenant," it means "to conclude a covenant"; used absolutely or with "kingdom," it means "to entrust, to assign."
G1303.portee: This verb reveals that God's covenant with His people is not imposed from the outside, but actively established and ordained by God Himself. It also shows the parallel between the testament of Christ (who had to die to become valid) and human testaments: the death of Christ gives definitive force to the new covenant. For the Christian, this reminds us that what he receives—the kingdom, grace, the law written on the heart—comes from a disposition of love, a specific will of God in his favor.

sens: to stay in a place, to spend time there
to dwell, to reside temporarily
to stay with someone, to keep them company
to rely on, to count on
G1304.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to physically stay somewhere for a period: Jesus "remained" in Judea with his disciples to teach and baptize (John 3:22), and Paul and Barnabas "remained" quite a while in Antioch preaching (Acts 15:35).
2. To dwell indicates a temporary presence, a time spent in a place, as when Herod "stayed" in Caesarea (Acts 12:19) or when one "spent" a few days in Philippi (Acts 16:12).
3. To stay with someone means to dedicate time to them, to be in their company: the apostles "remained quite a while" with the disciples in Iconium, sharing their lives and ministry (Acts 14:28).
4. Less often, the word evokes the idea of relying on or counting on someone: the apostles in Iconium spoke "relying on the Lord," meaning counting on His strength and testimony (Acts 14:3).
G1304.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to rub, to wear out" — the image is that of time being worn away, consumed by staying somewhere. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew "yashab" (to dwell, to inhabit) and "gour" (to stay with someone), which all retain the idea of remaining in place, establishing oneself for a period.
G1304.emploi: This verb appears nine times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Acts (eight occurrences) and once in John. It primarily describes the movements and temporary residences of the apostles: Paul and his companions "remain" in various cities to preach and teach (Antioch, Iconium, Philippi). The word can denote both a short presence ("to spend a few days") and a longer stay. In Acts 14:3, the meaning shifts towards the idea of relying on someone or counting on them, showing how the "duration" with a person implies trust in them.
G1304.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life unfolds in time and proximity: the apostles did not merely pass through cities, they "remained" there, building a community, teaching. It invites us to consider how we invest our time with others and with the Lord — not just passing by, but staying, rooting ourselves, relying on His strength for testimony.

sens: That which nourishes the body, what one eats and drinks
What is necessary for daily living
G1305.detail:
1. The word concretely refers to food, that is, what one eats and drinks to sustain the body. In 1 Timothy 6:8, Paul associates it with clothing: these are the two essential and minimal needs of a person to live with dignity.
2. More broadly, it evokes everything that is indispensable for maintaining daily life. Paul does not advocate seeking wealth or superfluous goods; it is enough to have food and clothing to be satisfied. It is a lesson in simplicity and contentment in the face of life's necessities.
G1305.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "diaetrephō," which means "to nourish" or "to sustain." The prefix "dia" (through, by) and the root "treph" (to nourish) together form the idea of nourishment that sustains life. This sense of sustenance also appears in the verb "trepho" (to nourish), used elsewhere in the New Testament. The word thus designates food as that which ensures the continuation of life.
G1305.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:8. Paul uses it to express a lesson of wisdom addressed to Timothy: in the context of the love of money and the temptations of wealth, the apostle reminds that if one has food and clothing, that is sufficient. This context shows that "food" means basic needs, distinct from desires for luxury or abundance. It is a call to sobriety and gratitude for the essentials.
G1305.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to distinguish between the necessary and the superfluous. In a culture of accumulation and covetousness, Paul redefines true wealth: it consists of having what is needed to live simply and decently, without seeking excess. This frees the heart to turn towards God rather than material goods. The Christian life is nourished first by true needs, both physical and spiritual, to learn contentment.

sens: To be tossed from side to side, to be shaken
To be scattered, spread out
To surpass in importance or quality
To have value, to be of interest
G1308.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to be transported, shaken from side to side. In Acts 27:27, Paul's ship is "tossed" on the Adriatic Sea — the boat sways, jostled by the waves.

2. The verb then takes on the meaning of "to spread," "to be disseminated." When Paul preaches in Acts 13:49, the word of God "spreads" throughout the region.

3. To surpass someone or something means to have a superior quality. Jesus asks in Matthew 6:26: "Are you not worth much more than the birds of the air?" — man has more value, more importance than the creatures he observes.

4. The word can also mean "to make a difference," "to matter." Paul reminds in Galatians 2:6 that "it does not matter" whether the great apostles liked him or not: it does not change his calling. This indicates that something "is important" or "is not."
G1308.origine: The word is composed of "dia" (through, from side to side) and "phérō" (to carry, to transport). The basic image is that of carrying across: first physically (from one point to another), then figuratively (to surpass, to have weight, to count). It is a dynamic word that emphasizes the action of surpassing or distinguishing oneself.
G1308.emploi: This verb appears 13 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and Paul. It is primarily used to say that someone or something "is worth more" than another: a man is worth more than a sheep (Matthew 12:12), you are worth more than the birds (Matthew 6:26, Luke 12:7). Paul uses it to express that certain things "matter" or "are not important" (Galatians 2:6). In Luke and Acts, it also describes the physical movement of being shaken or scattered. The word thus enriches itself with a nuance: beyond simple movement, it is to weigh in the balance, to have moral or existential weight.
G1308.portee: This word teaches the reader that human life has an incomparable value in the eyes of God. Jesus uses it to show that man should not fear: he counts much more than the birds, than the sheep. It is a word of encouragement: in the divine economy, you are not negligible. Furthermore, when Paul says that something does not "differ" or "matters little," he invites us to discern what truly counts from the perspective of the Gospel, against human criteria.

sens: To flee, to save oneself by passing through or beyond a danger
To succeed in not being affected by something
To survive a threat
G1309.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of fleeing, passing through a dangerous situation to reach safety. It is a movement that crosses the obstacle: one escapes *through* the danger, traversing it to come out on the other side. In Acts 27:42, the soldiers fear that the prisoners might escape by swimming, meaning they might overcome the peril of shipwreck by reaching the shore by swimming.

2. The word emphasizes the idea of success: not only does one flee, but one actually manages to escape, to not be captured or seized. It is escaping from something specific — a danger, a prison, a threat — and coming out alive.
G1309.origine: The word is composed of *dia* (through, by) and *pheugō* (to flee, to escape). This composition reinforces the idea: it is not simply fleeing, but fleeing *through*, passing from one side to the other of the danger. In the Greek Old Testament, equivalents such as *pālit* (fugitive, one who escapes) and *sārid* (survivor) can be found, which convey the same reality of salvation through flight.
G1309.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:42. In this context of Paul's shipwreck, the centurions want to kill the prisoners for fear that they might escape by swimming — that they might reach the shore by swimming and thus save themselves from the shipwreck. It is a dramatic moment where the escape would be salvation. The word carries all the tension of the moment: it is about an immediate danger from which one can escape.
G1309.portee: This word reminds us that in crises — spiritual or material — God can offer an escape. The believer who finds themselves facing danger or condemnation can hope for deliverance, an exit that will allow them to pass through. It is a call not to despair in the face of threats, for a safe escape remains possible.

sens: To spread, to publish information widely
To make known to many people
To propagate news or a rumor
G1310.detail: 1. This verb primarily means to spread or publish something far and wide, to make it widely known. In Mark 1:45, the healed man "begins to publish it widely and to disclose it," meaning he speaks about it openly and everywhere, so much so that Jesus has to withdraw to deserted places. 2. The word is also used to speak of a reputation that spreads: in Matthew 9:31, the blind men healed by Jesus "spread his fame throughout all the region." 3. It can refer to the spreading of a rumor or news, whether true or false: in Matthew 28:15, the false report of the soldiers has "spread among the Jews." In each case, it involves information that circulates and can no longer be contained.
G1310.origine: The Greek word combines the preposition "dia" (through) and "phêmê" (word, fame): the idea is to pass a word "through" people, to propagate it. It is a late verb in Greek, infrequent before the New Testament. It often translates the Hebrew "dabar" (word, thing, matter), which has the same meaning of transmitting news.
G1310.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels. In Matthew and Mark, it always describes the dissemination of news: either the healing of Jesus (Matthew 9:31, Mark 1:45) or a false report (Matthew 28:15). In each context, it highlights the power of words — they spread, escape control, and reach the crowds. In Mark 1:45, paradoxically, this disclosure prevents Jesus from continuing his public ministry in the towns.
G1310.portee: This word reminds the reader that words have a living force: they propagate, influence minds, shape opinion. It invites reflection on what we spread or allow to spread — good news or a lie — and on the weight of our testimony and language.

sens: To completely annihilate, ruin
To gradually damage, wear out
To sink, to go down
To morally corrupt, deprave
To spoil, to rot
G1311.detail:
1. To completely annihilate, ruin: it is to entirely destroy something. God threatens to destroy those who destroy the earth (Revelation 11:18), meaning to annihilate the destroyers.
2. To gradually damage, wear out: the word can refer to slow and gradual ruin. Our outer man is perishing day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16), as the body ages and wears out over time.
3. To sink, to go down: applied to ships and sea creatures, the word means to perish, to disappear. A third of the ships perish in judgment (Revelation 8:9).
4. To morally corrupt, deprave: it is to spoil the soul and understanding. The corrupt men of understanding are morally destroyed, their intelligence has been perverted away from the truth (1 Timothy 6:5).
5. To spoil, to rot: the concrete sense of the verb also applies to what naturally corrupts, like moths that destroy clothing (Luke 12:33).
G1311.origine: The Greek verb "diaphtheirô" is composed of the prefix "dia" (through, completely) and the verb "phtheirô" (to corrupt, to spoil). This composition intensifies the idea: it is not simply to damage, but to destroy thoroughly, completely. In Hebrew, this verb often translates the word "shâhat," which also means to corrupt, ruin, destroy. The family of the word includes the noun "phthora" (corruption, decay).
G1311.emploi: This verb appears five times in the New Testament, mostly in Revelation and the epistles. It is used in a physical sense: moths destroy clothing, ships perish, the body wears out (Luke 12:33, 2 Corinthians 4:16, Revelation 8:9). It is also used in a moral and spiritual sense: men are corrupted in their understanding, humanity destroys creation (1 Timothy 6:5, Revelation 11:18). The context of each occurrence shows whether the verb denotes brutal destruction, gradual wear, or corruption of the soul.
G1311.portee: This word reminds us that evil, in all its forms, destroys: perishable riches wear out and vanish, the body ages and weakens, the soul corrupts when it strays from the truth. For the believer, it underscores the importance of seeking a treasure that does not perish, a spiritual food that renews the inner man, and of keeping one's understanding pure before God.

sens: Physical destruction of a body
Fleshly decomposition after death
Rotting of the flesh
Moral or spiritual degradation
G1312.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes physical destruction, reduction to ruins: the image is that of something disintegrating, turning to dust. 2. More specifically, it refers to the corruption of a corpse, its decomposition in the grave: this is why the Segond regularly translates it as "corruption." Acts 2:27 speaks of the body of Christ not seeing corruption, meaning it would not experience the decay of the grave. 3. Acts 13:36 shows the contrast: David died and "saw corruption," while in Acts 13:37, the one whom God raised did "not see corruption" — a proof of the Resurrection. 4. By extension, the word can denote moral degradation or spiritual decline, everything that corrupts and deteriorates, although this usage is less visible in the provided verses.
G1312.origine: The word comes from the verb "διαφθείρω" (diaphtheirô), "to destroy completely," composed of "δια-" (dia-, "through," marking totality) and "φθείρω" (phtheirô), "to spoil, corrupt." This verb translates the Hebrew "שָׁחַת" (shachat), which also means "to destroy, corrupt." The Greek family includes the adjectives "φθαρτός" (corruptible) and "ἄφθαρτος" (incorruptible, which is used to speak of heavenly glory).
G1312.emploi: The word "corruption" appears 6 times in the New Testament, exclusively in Acts and always in relation to the resurrection of Christ. The three chapters of Peter (Acts 2) and Paul (Acts 13) together cite Psalm 16: the Christ will not be left "in the realm of the dead" and his flesh will "not see corruption." This is a major apologetic argument: the Resurrection of Christ, unlike the fate of any mortal man, preserved him from the physical degradation of death. David, on the other hand, died and "saw corruption," but the Resurrected did not see it — a living and bodily proof of his victory over death and God's redemptive plan.
G1312.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds of the stark reality of death: the human body returns to dust. But in apostolic preaching, it becomes the pivot of hope: the Resurrection of Christ breaks this universal law. It is not merely a spiritual survival, but a bodily restoration. Our own resurrection, promised to the Christian, follows the same pattern: Christ triumphed over corruption, and those who belong to him will triumph in turn.

sens: Distinguished by superior quality, surpassing
Different, varied, of diverse kinds
G1313.detail:
1. The word speaks of excellence, of superiority in quality. It is what prevails, what stands out. In Hebrews 1:4, the Son has become "so much better than the angels as he has inherited a more excellent name than theirs": his name reveals an incomparable greatness. Similarly, in Hebrews 8:6, Jesus has obtained a ministry "so much more excellent" as his covenant is better — the adjective here measures preeminence.
2. The word can also denote what is different, varied, diversified. In Hebrews 9:10, it refers to "various washings": purifications of different kinds, multiple, imposed under the old law. The idea is one of multiplicity and variation.
G1313.origine: The word comes from the preposition "dia" (through, separating) and "phérô" (to bear, to carry). It first evokes the idea of "bearing differently," hence "being different," then "to stand out," "to surpass," or "to be superior." It is an image of what exceeds, what separates from the common. In Hebrews, the same meaning is rendered by words like "yatar" (to excel) or by the idea of distinction and separation.
G1313.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, mostly in the Epistle to the Hebrews. In Romans 12:6, it qualifies the diverse gifts of God: "having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us." In Hebrews, it takes on two nuances. In chapters 1:4 and 8:6, it expresses the superiority of Christ: his name and ministry are "more excellent" than those of the angels or the old covenant. In Hebrews 9:10, it denotes the diversity of ritual practices of the Old Testament. The context thus directs the meaning toward excellence or variety.
G1313.portee: This word reminds believers that Christ occupies a unique, incomparable place, above all. His excellence is not just a theological assertion, but a reality that transforms our relationship with him and with faith. It also invites us to recognize the variety of gifts and calls that God distributes to each Christian.

sens: To protect someone by watching over them attentively
To actively defend against danger
G1314.detail:
1. To keep means to watch over someone with attention and care, like a guardian or sentinel who does not leave their post. The word evokes the image of constant and vigilant protection. In Luke 4:10, Jesus quotes a psalm: the angels "will keep you," meaning they watch over you without ceasing.
2. To keep can also mean to actively defend, to care for someone by putting them out of harm's way. It is less about simple surveillance than about the commitment to truly protect against the dangers that threaten them.
G1314.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to protect" or "to secure." The prefix "dia-" (through, completely) reinforces the idea: it is about comprehensive and uninterrupted protection. In Hebrew, the verb "shâmar" (שָׁמַר) often carries the same image of attentive vigilance and entrusted guarding.
G1314.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:10, where Jesus refers to Psalm 91:11. The context is the temptation in the desert: Satan proposes to Jesus to throw himself from the temple, trusting in the promise that the angels will "keep" him. This passage shows that "to keep" denotes the divine protection assured by God's messengers. The verb emphasizes here a permanent angelic vigilance over God's people.
G1314.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God does not abandon them: he entrusts their keeping to his angels who watch over them ceaselessly. It is an invitation to trust in divine protection, not to relieve us of wisdom, but to assure us that we are under the gaze of the Heavenly Father.

sens: To kill, to take life
To arrest and execute someone
G1315.detail:
1. To kill means to take someone's life. The word evokes the idea of laying hands on a person to eliminate them. In Acts 5:30, Peter accuses the Jewish leaders of having killed Jesus by hanging him on a tree — this is the direct accusation of the murder of the Messiah.
2. To arrest and execute means to seize someone to put them to death. In Acts 26:21, Paul recounts that the Jews seized him in the temple and attempted to kill him — this refers to an attempted execution, a violent action to eliminate him.
G1315.origine: The word comes from the Greek χείρ (khéir), "hand." The prefix διά- (dia-) means "through": the basic image is that of "handling with hands," hence "to conduct, to manage," and in later usage (among Greek historians and Jewish writers), "to lay hands on," "to strike" until "to kill." It is a relatively rare word, used mainly in contexts of execution or violent acts.
G1315.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts, at critical moments when the apostles speak of the death of Jesus and threats against their own lives. In Acts 5:30, it is the direct accusation made by Peter against those who crucified Jesus. In Acts 26:21, it is Paul's account before Agrippa of the Jews' attempt to eliminate him in the temple. The verb translates either "to kill" or "to perish" (in the sense of being killed), depending on the construction and context.
G1315.portee: This word reminds us that the crucifixion of Jesus was an act of deliberate violence, a willful killing, not a misfortune or accident. It also invites the reader to see the courage of the apostles: they accept the very possibility of dying to bear witness to their faith. For the Christian, this word measures the cost of the Gospel — the spilled blood of the Master and the risk faced by his witnesses.

sens: To leave by detaching oneself from a person or a group
To physically leave a place or a community
G1316.detail:
1. This verb describes the action of detaching and distancing oneself from someone or something. It is a clear, complete separation marked by distance. In Luke 9:33, the disciples separate from Jesus at the moment he descends from the Mount of Transfiguration — they detach themselves to return to the reality of the crowd waiting for them.
2. The word can also simply express the act of physically leaving a place or a group to go elsewhere. The separation here is less a rupture than a natural departure, a crossing of distance.
G1316.origine: The Greek word is composed of "dia" (through, in two) and "chorizō" (to separate, to set apart). This root evokes the image of a line that divides, creating space between two things. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, words like "badal" (to separate) and "parad" (to disperse) express a similar idea of division or distinction. The Greek of the Septuagint uses it notably in Genesis 1:4, where God separates the light from the darkness — a total and definitive separation.
G1316.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 9:33. It is found in the account of the Transfiguration: at the moment when Jesus, Moses, and Elijah are about to separate from Peter, James, and John (the time of the vision coming to an end), Peter asks to stay. The context is that of a divine moment coming to an end and returning to ordinary life. Peter wants to prolong this heavenly experience, while separation is imminent.
G1316.portee: This word reminds us that moments of grace with God have an earthly end — the mystical experience must give way to ordinary service. At the same time, separation is never a final rupture: Jesus descends with his disciples to face the world. It is an invitation to accept times of spiritual rest while remaining attached to the daily path of faith.

sens: Capable of instructing, transmitting teaching with clarity and effectiveness
Able to train disciples or students
Gifted with patience and kindness in instruction
G1317.detail:
1. The word describes a concrete ability: that of explaining well, of communicating a doctrine in a way that others understand. It is an aptitude for teaching, not merely knowledge kept to oneself. In 1 Timothy 3:2, the bishop must be "apt to teach," meaning capable of instructing his Church well.
2. It is also a disposition to train others, to lead them progressively toward understanding. The Lord's servant in 2 Timothy 2:24 must be "apt to teach," capable of patience and kindness toward those who have not yet grasped the truths of the Gospel.
3. The adjective implies a moral gentleness: one can only teach well if one knows how to listen, to welcome questions, to master impatience. This is why the text associates it with patience and the ability to endure disputes without responding with quarrels.
G1317.origine: The word comes from the root "didack-" which means to teach or to learn. It is formed as an adjective indicating aptitude, capacity: "didaktikos" = "capable of didachè," that is, capable of transmitting doctrine. It is a technical term in Christian vocabulary, particularly valued in the pastoral epistles that define the qualities of church leaders.
G1317.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two epistles to Timothy, which deal with the organization of the local Church and the training of leaders. In 1 Timothy 3:2, it is an essential quality of the bishop (overseer), placed at the heart of his ideal profile. In 2 Timothy 2:24, it characterizes the Lord's servant in the face of opponents: he must not seek quarrels, but remain capable of teaching, that is, patient and kind. The context emphasizes the balance between doctrinal firmness and pedagogical gentleness.
G1317.portee: For today's Christian, this word reminds us that the ministry of teaching is not a raw gift, but a capacity that is cultivated through gentleness, listening, and patience. It invites community leaders to examine not only whether they know the doctrine but whether they can communicate it with respect and tenderness. It is also a call to all believers who wish to share their faith: teaching is first about seeking to serve the listener, not to impress or dominate.

sens: Who can be taught, capable of learning
Who has received instruction, formed by someone
Inspired or instructed by a divine or spiritual source
G1318.detail:
1. The word first describes what is susceptible to being taught, that is, what can be the subject of learning. It is the idea of the capacity to receive instruction.

2. It then designates one who has actually received instruction, who bears its mark. In John 6:45, Jesus cites the prophet saying that believers will be "taught by God" — they will have personally received divine instruction.

3. Finally, it qualifies what comes directly from a spiritual source rather than a human source. In 1 Corinthians 2:13, Paul contrasts the "words taught by the Spirit" with the "words taught by human wisdom": these words bear the imprint of the Holy Spirit who formed them.
G1318.origine: The word comes from the Greek root διδάσκω (didaskô), which means "to teach." The suffix -τος indicates a passive state: something that has undergone the action. This is why διδακτός (didaktos) evokes one who has been shaped by teaching, marked by received instruction. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "limoud," which also expresses the idea of being instructed or formed.
G1318.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In John 6:45, it qualifies the disciples of the Father — all those whom God personally instructs are drawn to Jesus. In 1 Corinthians 2:13, it characterizes the words or language of the apostle: Paul asserts that his teaching is not based on human rhetoric, but on the instruction that the Holy Spirit gives him. In both cases, the word emphasizes the divine origin of the instruction, not its transmission by purely natural or human means.
G1318.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that true teaching comes from God, not from mere human reason. It reminds us that becoming a disciple is first about being formed by God himself, and that true wisdom — the kind that the apostle Paul proclaims — bears the mark of the Holy Spirit. It is a call to listen to God rather than relying solely on the opinions of the world.

sens: The act of teaching, communicating knowledge or truth
The content of this teaching, what is taught
A set of principles or beliefs received and transmitted
The quality or manner of teaching
Teaching that conforms to divine truth, opposed to false doctrines
G1319.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the act of teaching, the action by which knowledge is transmitted: in 1 Timothy 4:13, Paul urges Timothy to focus on reading, exhortation, and teaching — three ways to edify the church.
2. It can also refer to what is taught, the message or instruction itself: in Romans 15:4, "everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction," meaning to teach us lessons that give us hope.
3. The word takes on a broader shade when it refers to a doctrine, a body of principles: in 1 Timothy 1:10, it refers to "sound doctrine," that is, the coherent set of Christian truth, as opposed to lies.
4. Sometimes the word emphasizes the quality of the one who teaches: in Titus 2:7, Titus himself must be a model by showing integrity "in teaching."
5. The Bible often contrasts sound doctrine with false doctrines: in 1 Timothy 4:1, there are "doctrines of demons," and in Colossians 2:22, there are "doctrines of men" — deceptive teachings that lead away from the truth.
G1319.origine: The word comes from the verb διδάσκω (didaskô), which means "to teach." It primarily denotes the action, and then gradually the result of that action: what is taught and retained. In Hebrew, the word is often rendered by לָמַד (lamad), "to learn" or "to teach," which speaks of the process of transmitting knowledge. The Greek διδασκαλία emphasizes that teaching is a living reality: it is what passes between a teacher and his disciples.
G1319.emploi: This word appears 21 times in the New Testament, especially in the pastoral epistles (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) and in the Pauline epistles. It refers sometimes to the act of teaching in the church (Romans 12:7, 1 Timothy 4:13), and sometimes to Christian teaching considered as a treasure to keep (1 Timothy 6:1). Paul emphasizes "sound doctrine," that is, teaching that builds faith: in 1 Timothy 1:10 and 2 Timothy 4:3, it is about rejecting false doctrines and myths. Biblical teaching is alive: it corrects, instructs, comforts (2 Timothy 3:16). The word also shows that doctrine is never neutral — it comes either from God, from men, or even from demons (1 Timothy 4:1).
G1319.portee: This word reminds Christians that faith is not a vague feeling, but a solid teaching to know and live. It calls us to discern: to receive sound doctrine and reject false doctrines that deceive. It is also a responsibility: those who teach must be vigilant about the quality of what they transmit, for teaching shapes lives and churches.

sens: one who teaches, who transmits knowledge
one who has authority, who directs or commands
a respectful title of address towards someone wise or of high rank
a figure of spiritual authority and wisdom
G1320.detail:
1. A master is one who teaches and transmits knowledge to others. This is the primary meaning: a schoolmaster or a spiritual teacher who trains his disciples. In Luke 2:46, the teachers of the temple listen to the child Jesus and ask him questions, showing that they are teaching.
2. The word also designates a figure of authority to whom one obeys. In Matthew 10:24, it is said that a disciple is not above his master: there is a relationship of command and submission.
3. It is a courteous and respectful title of address towards someone of distinction. People use it when addressing Jesus or the scribes to mark their respect, as in Matthew 8:19 where a scribe says to Jesus: "Master, I will follow you everywhere."
4. The word takes on a spiritual significance when it refers to Jesus or the teachers of the Church: it is a guide who does not merely transmit ideas, but shapes the heart and faith of his disciples, as in John 13:13-14 where Jesus claims to be master and shows his authority by washing the feet of his disciples.
G1320.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "didaskô" which means "to teach" or "to instruct." It is a compound word: the root evokes the idea of showing, demonstrating, transmitting knowledge in a visible and practical way. The Hebrew word "rabbi" (master, lord) often translates it in the context of the New Testament. It is an honorific title in Jewish tradition, emphasizing the authority of the one who teaches the Law and wisdom.
G1320.emploi: The word "master" appears 58 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. It is first used for Jesus: the disciples and the crowd call him this (Matthew 8:19, John 3:2), particularly when they plead with him or seek his counsel. It is also applied to the scribes and Pharisees who teach the Law (Luke 2:46, John 3:10), and even to John the Baptist (Luke 3:12). The early Church also applies it to those who have the gift of teaching (1 Corinthians 12:28-29, Ephesians 4:11). The word slightly changes nuance: in Matthew and Mark, it is often the title shouted towards Jesus to gain his attention or help; in John, it expresses a deeper recognition of his spiritual authority (John 13:13). Paul uses it to speak of his own ministry (2 Timothy 1:11) and to designate the teachers of the Church.
G1320.portee: The word "master" reminds Christians that Jesus is the one who teaches, not only through words but through his example and authority. Recognizing Jesus as master means accepting to be his disciple and learning from him. For those who teach in the Church, this word is also a call to humility: a master must remain a disciple, attentive to the will of his Master.

sens: To transmit teaching, a doctrine to someone
To instruct someone in the knowledge of something
To preach, publicly proclaim a message
To act as a master, exercise the authority of one who instructs
G1321.detail:
1. To teach is primarily to transmit knowledge or a doctrine to a person or group. It is the action of the master in front of his disciples: Jesus "taught" in the synagogues (Matthew 4:23), meaning he communicated his message. One can also teach a specific thing: "Teaching in the name of Jesus" (Acts 4:18) means proclaiming the message of Christ.
2. Teaching often involves the idea of instructing, forming someone in the truth. When Paul writes, "you who teach others, do you not teach yourself?" (Romans 2:21), he refers to the role of one who guides others toward the right knowledge.
3. To teach can mean to preach or publicly proclaim, especially a religious or moral content. Jesus "taught in the temple" (Luke 21:37), which includes preaching intended for the gathered people.
4. The verb carries a dimension of authority: Mark notes that Jesus "taught as one having authority, and not as the scribes" (Mark 1:22), meaning he spoke as a master, not merely as a reporter of traditions.
G1321.origine: The Greek word didaskō comes from a root that evokes the idea of showing, making known. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew verb "lamad" (to teach, to learn), which shares the same notion of learning and transmission. It is an active verb that implies a relationship between the one who knows and the one who learns: the master transmits not only knowledge but also a way of understanding and living.
G1321.emploi: The verb to teach appears about 91 times in the New Testament, very frequently in the Gospels to describe the central activity of Jesus. At the beginning of his ministry, "Jesus went throughout all Galilee, teaching in the synagogues" (Matthew 4:23); he is found throughout his public life teaching in the temple (Luke 21:37, John 8:2). The Gospels emphasize that Jesus taught "with authority" (Mark 1:22), which distinguished his teaching from that of the scribes. After the Resurrection, the apostles are arrested for continuing to "teach in the name of Jesus" (Acts 4:18). Paul also speaks of it as a gift and a responsibility of church leaders (Romans 12:7; 1 Corinthians 4:17). The verb is used sometimes with a complement of person (who is being taught?), sometimes with that of doctrine (what is being taught?), and sometimes absolutely (there is a teaching being given).
G1321.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that Jesus came first as a master, not as a legislator: he teaches the truth, shapes hearts, transforms minds. The authority of Jesus resides in the word, not in force. This also means that becoming a Christian is entering into a learning process: one receives the teaching, understands it, and lives it. The Church, inheritor of this mission, has the role of continuing this teaching (Matthew 28:20) — not to impose, but to enlighten and form.

sens: What is taught, the set of truths or principles transmitted by a master
The act of teaching, the transmission of knowledge
The authority and power with which one teaches
A coherent set of beliefs or particular teachings
G1322.detail:
1. Doctrine is primarily the content of teaching — the set of truths that are transmitted. Jesus teaches a new doctrine (Mark 1:27), so powerful that the crowd is astonished. This doctrine can be that of Jesus, that of the apostles, or even that of other masters: it is what comes from the mouth of the master and imprints itself in the mind of the listener (Matthew 7:28).

2. Doctrine is also the act of teaching itself, the activity of the master. The apostles persist in teaching (Acts 2:42), Timothy must instruct others (2 Timothy 4:2). It is the same word that covers both what comes from the master (the doctrine) and the act by which he transmits it.

3. Often, doctrine carries with it remarkable authority. Jesus spoke with authority (Luke 4:32), and it was not the authority of the scribe who repeats, but that of one who possesses the truth. This doctrine strikes, astonishes, and even commands unclean spirits (Mark 1:27).

4. Doctrine can designate a particular set of beliefs or principles — the doctrine of the Pharisees (Matthew 16:12), the doctrine of the Balaamites (Revelation 2:14). It also refers to the doctrine of baptism (Hebrews 6:2), meaning the set of truths that form its core.
G1322.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to teach." Its initial image is that of someone who transmits knowledge, distributing it to others. In Hebrew, the Old Testament Bible uses a root that means "to teach" or "to point out" (in the Greek Septuagint, an ancient version). The word designates both the teaching given and the act of teaching — in ancient Greek, the same word can cover these two facets of the same reality.
G1322.emploi: Doctrine appears 29 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and the epistles. In Matthew, Mark, and Luke, it is often the doctrine of Jesus that strikes the crowds with its authority — it teaches differently from the scribes (Mark 1:22). In John and in Acts, we speak of the teaching of the apostles and what must be kept. In the epistles (Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Timothy, Titus, Hebrews), doctrine becomes the set of Christian principles to defend, to teach, and not to abandon. Revelation warns against false doctrines — that of Balaam (Revelation 2:14), that of the Nicolaitans (Revelation 2:15). The word thus takes on color according to the context: power with Jesus, faithfulness with the apostles, guarding and transmission with church leaders.
G1322.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that faith is not a vague feeling, but a set of truths to know and keep. Jesus did not come to evoke emotions, but to teach — and this doctrine carries authority because it comes from God. The word also invites us to distinguish good doctrines from false ones: there is a doctrine of Christ to receive, and doctrines of men to reject. Finally, it calls the believer not to abandon what has been established, but to root himself in it and transmit it.

sens: Greek coin worth two regular drachmas
Temple tax in Jewish tradition, equivalent to half a shekel
G1323.detail:
1. The double drachma is a Greek coin whose value corresponds to two ordinary drachmas. It was a common circulating currency in the Greek and Mediterranean world during the New Testament period. In Matthew 17:24, Jesus and his disciples are asked to pay this tax in Capernaum.
2. This double drachma also served as the Jewish Temple tax, known as the Temple tax. It was approximately equivalent to half a shekel, the annual contribution that each Israelite was required to pay for the maintenance of the Temple. This is what the collectors demand in Matthew 17:24: "Does your master not pay the two drachmas?"
G1323.origine: The Greek word δίδραχμος is composed of δίς ("twice") and δραχμή ("drachma"). The drachma itself is an ancient Greek monetary unit. In the Septuagint, this coin translates notably the Hebrew shekel (שֶׁקֶל), the standard currency of the ancient Near East. The half-shekel of the Temple corresponds precisely to the double drachma, illustrating how the Greek monetary system adapted to Jewish religious obligations.
G1323.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 17:24. It is in the famous episode where Jesus arrives in Capernaum and the Temple tax collectors ask Peter if Jesus will pay the "two drachmas." This specific context — the Temple taxation — shows that the term refers not only to a coin of double value but also to a well-defined civil and religious contribution. Jesus responds miraculously: he asks Peter to catch a fish that will have a coin in its mouth sufficient to pay this tax (Matthew 17:27).
G1323.portee: This episode reveals Jesus' attitude toward legal obligations: he does not refuse to pay the Temple tax, but he does so in a sovereign and miraculous manner, affirming his freedom and authority. For the believer, this teaches that Jesus does not contest civil and religious duties but fulfills them with an authority that transcends mere submission. It is a lesson in practical wisdom: to respect established laws while recognizing the lordship of Christ.

sens: Nickname of the apostle Thomas, meaning "twin" in Greek
G1324.detail: Didymus is the Greek nickname of Thomas, one of the twelve apostles of Jesus. This nickname, derived from the Greek word meaning "double" or "twin," suggests that Thomas likely had a twin brother, or that this name was given for a similar reason. John is the only evangelist to mention this nickname: he uses it three times to refer to Thomas — in John 11:16 during the resurrection of Lazarus, in John 20:24 when Thomas is absent from the first resurrected appearance of Jesus, and in John 21:2 during an appearance by the Sea of Tiberias.
G1324.origine: The Greek word Didymos comes from the adjective didymos, -ē, -on, which literally means "double" or "twin." It is a nickname that likely reflects a physical or familial reality of Thomas, transformed into a personal designation. John uses this nickname to clearly identify this disciple among the other apostles of the same name.
G1324.emploi: Thomas, called Didymus, is one of the twelve apostles of Jesus mentioned only in the Gospel of John. He appears in three key passages: in John 11:16, he shows his devotion by suggesting to go with Jesus to Bethany despite the danger; in John 20:24, he is noted as absent during the first resurrected appearance, which later places him in the famous doubt; in John 21:2, he is listed among the disciples gathered at the Sea of Tiberias after the resurrection. The nickname Didymus always appears associated with Thomas, never isolated, emphasizing his distinct identity within the apostolic group.
G1324.portee: Didymus reminds us that even the apostles had nicknames and personal stories that only certain evangelists preserved. The repeated mention of this nickname by John invites the reader to see Thomas as a singular character: courageous when it is necessary to face danger, authentic in doubt, and faithful in his conversion to the resurrection of the Lord.

sens: to hand something to someone
to confer power, authority, ability
to provide what is necessary, to nourish
to present, to offer for viewing or consumption
to yield, to deliver into the hands of
to produce a result
G1325.detail:
1. To hand something to someone: the simplest and most common meaning. It is to pass an object or thing to a person so that they possess or use it. "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11): this is asking God to provide us with what we need each day.
2. To confer power, authority, ability: going beyond the material object, it is to grant someone the right or strength to do something. "Jesus gave them power to cast out unclean spirits" (Matthew 10:1): he confers spiritual authority to the disciples.
3. To provide what is necessary, to nourish or sustain: it is to give so that life continues. "No one gave him anything" (Luke 15:16): the prodigal son has nothing to eat, no one gives him the food he needs.
4. To present, to offer for viewing or consumption: to show, to make known or to serve something. "Jesus took the bread, and after giving thanks, he broke it and gave it to them" (Matthew 26:26): he presents the bread for them to eat.
5. To yield, to deliver into the hands of: to abandon someone or something to the power of another. "He who betrays me is delivering me" (Matthew 26:48): Judas delivers Jesus to his enemies.
6. To produce a result, to participate in a production: it is to bear fruit or generate something. "A good soil...produced fruit" (Mark 4:8): the seed gives its harvest, it bears fruit.
G1325.origine: The verb δίδωμι (didōmi) comes from a very ancient Indo-European root, that of sharing and distribution. In Hebrew, it primarily translates נָתַן (natan), which also means to give, to hand over, to deliver: it is a verb of transfer from one hand to another. The Greek δίδωμι expresses this same idea of an action passing from a subject to an object, and often from one person to another. The same family is found in δῶρον (doron, the gift) and δωρέομαι (dōreomai, to make a present): all speak of generosity and sharing.
G1325.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the New Testament: 378 occurrences. It appears in all the Gospels, the Acts, and the epistles, always with the notion of transfer or provision. The context varies: giving bread or water (food), giving life or authority (power), giving a name or knowledge (information), giving one's body or blood (sacrifice). In the Gospel of John, it takes on a particular hue: God the Father "gives" believers to the Son (John 6:37), and the Son "gives" eternal life. In Matthew 10:8, Jesus says, "Freely you have received, freely give": this is the principle of sharing and generosity. The verb is also used in the passive or in compounds to express what is handed over, delivered, or entrusted.
G1325.portee: This verb touches the heart of the Gospel: God is the great giver. He gives life, food, wisdom, forgiveness, his Son himself. Understanding the nuances of "to give" in the Bible helps the reader grasp God's generosity toward us and to imitate that generosity toward others. It also recognizes that we own nothing of our own: everything is received, therefore everything can and should be shared. The promise "he will give you" in response to prayer (John 16:23) underpins the believer's trust in divine provision.

sens: To come out of sleep, to wake up
To put in motion, to stir
To excite, to stimulate attention or reflection
G1326.detail:
1. To awaken someone from sleep or a deep state of rest: Jesus sleeps in the boat during the storm, and the disciples wake him by shouting, "Master, Master, we are perishing!" (Luke 8:24). Once awakened, he calms the raging sea. This is the most literal and concrete sense of the word.
2. To put in motion or stir, especially in reference to nature or elements: the sea was stirred by a great wind (John 6:18), the waves rise and stir. The word here describes the action of moving, shaking, exciting something that was calm.
3. To excite, stimulate the mind or memory, to awaken someone's attention to a truth: Peter writes to keep his readers alert with warnings (2 Peter 1:13), to awaken their understanding (2 Peter 3:1). The word is used figuratively to denote the action of making someone attentive, aware, internally mobilized.
G1326.origine: The word comes from the Greek prefix "dia" (through, completely) combined with "egeirō" (to awaken, to raise). This composition emphasizes the action from one end to the other, completely and energetically. The root verb evokes the idea of rising or standing up. The notion of moving from one state to another — from sleep to wakefulness, from calm to agitation, from inattentiveness to awareness — is at the heart of the word.
G1326.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament. In the three Synoptic Gospels, it first describes the concrete action of waking Jesus who is asleep during the storm on the lake (Mark 4:39, Luke 8:24). John uses it to describe the agitation of the sea stirred by the wind (John 6:18). In the two letters of Peter, the verb shifts to a figurative register: Peter uses it to speak of his intention to keep his readers spiritually alert, to stimulate them with warnings, and to maintain their attention focused on Christian truths. The word thus glides from the physical and sensory to the spiritual and intellectual.
G1326.portee: This word invites us to recognize that we can be spiritually asleep, inattentive to God's warnings and the calls of the Holy Spirit. Like the disciples who sleep during the storm, we need to be awakened to the reality of danger and the power of Christ. For the Christian reader, Peter's word takes on a personal significance: stay vigilant, do not let your conscience fall asleep on the truths of the Gospel. There is an urgency to remain spiritually awake.

sens: Intersection of paths
Point of convergence of several ways
Place of passage where several roads meet
G1327.detail:
1. The word literally designates an intersection of paths, a place where several roads meet and cross. It is a strategic passage, a point of convergence. In Matthew 22:9, Jesus tells the servants to go "to the crossroads" to invite passersby to the wedding: this is where people circulate, a natural meeting place.
2. By extension, it is a very busy public passage, where travelers, merchants, and beggars stop and mingle. It is a visible place, accessible to all, ideal for meeting the crowd.
G1327.origine: The Greek word combines "dia" (through, by) and "exodos" (exit, way out), literally "passage through." It describes the idea of paths crossing, a place where one can go in several directions. The Hebrew "tôtzaah" (exit) is close to this notion, as shown in its use in descriptions of territories in Numbers and Joshua, where it designates exits, boundaries, or crossroads of the territory.
G1327.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 22:9, in the parable of the wedding feast. Jesus teaches that the Kingdom of God is intended only for chosen guests, but when they refuse, the master sends his servants to seek guests everywhere: "at the crossroads." It is the prime location to meet the crowd, the insignificant, ordinary people. The context emphasizes accessibility: one goes where the people are, to public places of passage.
G1327.portee: This image of the crossroads reminds us that the Gospel must reach everyone, without distinction, wherever people are — not just the elites or the well-to-do, but also the poor, the outcasts, those who happen to be there. It invites the believer to go to others where they truly are, rather than waiting for them.

sens: one who translates the words from one language to another so that listeners can understand
one who explains the meaning of something obscure or misunderstood
G1328.detail:
1. The interpreter is primarily the person who translates spoken words from one language into another, so that those who do not understand the first can hear and grasp the message. It is a role of a mediator: he carries the word of a person to the ears of his listeners in their own idiom. In the Church of Corinth, when someone spoke in unknown tongues, the interpreter was the one who made this word intelligible to all (1 Corinthians 14:28).
2. By extension, the interpreter can also be one who explains and clarifies what is confusing, enigmatic, or misunderstood — one who helps to understand the true meaning of a word or event.
G1328.origine: The word comes from the Greek διερμηνεύω (diermēneuō), which means "to translate, to interpret, to explain." It is composed of the prefix διά (dia, "through") and ἑρμηνεύω (hermēneuō, "to interpret"). The root evokes the idea of passing a message through a barrier — the barrier of language — so that the meaning is fully received on the other side. The god Hermes, messenger of the gods in Greek mythology, shares the same family of words.
G1328.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 14:28. Paul addresses an issue of order in the Christian assembly: when someone spoke in tongues — a mysterious and unintelligible word to others — an interpreter needed to be present for this gift of the Spirit to serve the common edification. If no interpreter was available, it was better to remain silent. The term emphasizes the importance of the service rendered: it is through the interpreter that the charismatic word becomes useful to the whole body.
G1328.portee: This word reminds Christians that every spiritual gift has a communal purpose. One does not speak only for oneself, but so that others may be edified and understand. It also invites us to value those who, without spectacular gifts, serve the Church by making the word and meaning clear: translators, explainers, educators. It is a humble yet firm word from Paul: the charismatic needs the translator, and both are essential.

sens: Explain the meaning of a text or a word by commenting on it
Translate or make known the meaning of a word in another language
Give the meaning of a name or a foreign expression
G1329.detail:
1. Explain a text or words: this involves uncovering the hidden or profound meaning. In Luke 24:27, Jesus "interpreted" to the disciples, starting from Moses and the prophets, all that concerned him in the Scriptures — he revealed the messianic meaning that they did not see.
2. Translate or make intelligible what has been said in another language or in an enigmatic way, especially in worship: in 1 Corinthians 14:5 and 14:13, the one who speaks in tongues must "interpret" his words so that the assembly can understand and be edified.
3. Give the meaning of a name or expression: in Acts 9:36, we are told that Tabitha "means" Dorcas — the Greek word clarifies the meaning of the Aramaic name.
G1329.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἐρμηνεύω (hermēneuō: interpret), preceded by the prefix διά (dia) which reinforces or deepens the action. Hermes, the messenger god, shares the same root — to interpret is to convey a message, to transfer it from one form to another. The word expresses the idea of revealing, explicating what was hidden or obscure.
G1329.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, always in contexts where clarity is needed for what is not clear. In the Gospel of Luke, it describes the messianic exegesis that Jesus performs on the Scriptures. In Paul's epistles (1 Corinthians 12-14), it appears 4 times regarding the gift of interpretation of tongues: Paul emphasizes the importance of this gift for the edification of the Church — interpreting is not a secondary gift; it is translating an incomprehensible divine word into a comprehensible and useful word. Once (Acts 9:36), it simply translates a proper name.
G1329.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith rests on the understanding of the divine message. Jesus himself had to "interpret" the Old Testament to open the eyes of his disciples to the mystery of his salvation. In the life of the Church, the gift of interpretation ensures that what comes from God is received clearly and is useful to all — there is no spiritual word without clarity. It is a call to serve others by making God's will accessible.

sens: Move from one place to another by crossing an area, an intermediate place
Travel through a region, visiting places successively
Spread, disseminate (for news, a rumor)
Cross something in a way that pierces or penetrates it
G1330.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to cross an area: to go from one side to the other of an obstacle or region. Jesus says, "He had to pass through Samaria" (John 4:4), which means that the route from Judea to Galilee passed through this territory. It also means passing through doors or obstacles: Peter "passed" through the prison gate (Acts 12:10).
2. To travel means to systematically journey from one place to another, visiting an entire region. Paul, "after traveling through the high provinces of Asia, arrived at Ephesus" (Acts 19:1): he crossed and visited several cities. It is also the movement of someone going from place to place: Jesus "went about doing good" (Acts 10:38).
3. For news or a rumor, the word means to spread, to disseminate everywhere. "The news of his healing spread everywhere" (Luke 5:15): the word spread like someone crossing regions.
4. Figuratively, to cross can mean to pierce or penetrate: the sword "pierced the soul" of Mary (Luke 2:35), meaning the pain completely pierced her like a blade.
G1330.origine: The Greek word comes from the prefix δι- ("through") and the verb ἔρχομαι ("to go, to come"). This combination creates the image of crossing while going. Latin often translates this word with forms of "permeate" or "transire." In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew אֵבֶר ("to pass"), הָלַךְ ("to walk"), and בּוֹא ("to come"), showing that it covers the entire biblical idea of movement through spaces.
G1330.emploi: This verb appears 43 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It describes the movements of Jesus and the apostles: Jesus crosses the lake (Luke 8:22), passes through Samaria (John 4:4), and goes from city to city. Acts regularly uses it for the missionary journeys of Peter and Paul: Paul "traveled" through Asia (Acts 19:1), the disciples "went" from place to place (Acts 8:4, 8:40). The word also takes on a figurative meaning: an unclean spirit "goes" through arid places (Luke 12:43), a rumor "spreads" (Luke 5:15), pain "pierces" the soul (Luke 2:35). Paul uses it metaphorically for Christ who "has passed through" the heavens (Hebrews 4:14).
G1330.portee: This verb reminds us that Christ and his disciples were on the move, not waiting in one place: the Christian faith is movement, testimony that spreads, service that traverses the world. It also illustrates the fragility of the human soul exposed to the crossing of suffering, and the power of Christ who crosses obstacles to save us.

sens: Seek to know something through questions or research
Discover information by asking here and there
Know where to find someone or something by asking questions
G1331.detail:
1. The word primarily means to seek to learn something by questioning, actively investigating. It is not simply hearing about something passively, but making the effort to ask questions to understand or know well. In Acts 10:17, Cornelius' servants inquire about the house of Simon: they ask where he lives, seeking by questioning the local residents.
2. The idea of discovering is added to that of questioning: it is through inquiry that one eventually knows or finds out. The men sent did not know where Simon was staying; by inquiring with neighbors or passersby, they discover and locate his house.
G1331.origine: The Greek word is composed of "dia" (through, everywhere) and "erotaō" (to question, to ask). This composition suggests an inquiry that goes everywhere, questioning from all sides to arrive at knowing. The root "erotaō" belongs to the family of verbs that denote serious questioning and interrogation. The simple verb "erotaō" means to ask, to question; by prefixing it with "dia," the idea of systematic searching, of in-depth questioning is added.
G1331.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 10:17. This is a crucial moment in the story of Cornelius: Peter has had a vision that troubled his mind, and during this time, the three men sent by Cornelius to seek him arrive in Joppa. The text says they had inquired about the house of Simon the tanner, meaning they had conducted a local inquiry to locate the place where the master they were seeking lived. This verb emphasizes the active and deliberate aspect of their search: they did not wander aimlessly, but they asked questions and sought information to accomplish their mission.
G1331.portee: This word reminds us that faith is often accompanied by active and honest searching. Cornelius' servants do not remain passive: they inquire, they seek, they act to obey their master. For the reader, it is an invitation not to remain indifferent to what one does not know, but to seek to learn, to ask questions, and to investigate for better understanding. It is also an image of the first mission: the Gentiles themselves actively seek to join the people of God and to hear his message.

sens: Who has reached the age of two years
Child of the second birthday
G1332.detail:
1. The adjective designates what has lasted or lasts two years, but in the Bible, it mainly applies to age: a child "of two years" has reached their full two years. In Matthew 2:16, Herod orders the massacre of all children "two years old and under" in Bethlehem — these are toddlers, infants, and young children who have not yet surpassed this age.
2. The expression "from two years" (Greek: "ἀπὸ διετής") emphasizes that the king is targeting a specific age range: he wants to eliminate the potential rival by killing all children who could have been born around the time of the visit of the Magi, roughly from birth up to about two years.
G1332.origine: The word comes from two simple Greek elements: "dis" (two) and "etos" (year, age). It is an adjective formed on the model of duration adjectives: "trimester" comes from three months, "semester" from six months. In English, we say "biannual" or "biennial" for something that occurs every two years. The Greek constructs directly "two-year" to describe a child or object aged two years.
G1332.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek Bible: Matthew 2:16, during the massacre of the Innocents. Herod, learning from the Magi that a king of the Jews has been born, seeks to destroy this newborn rival. To ensure he does not miss him, he orders the execution of all children "two years old and under" in the region of Bethlehem — a massive cruelty directed against the most vulnerable. This unique context shows the word applied to the dramatic condition of innocent children caught in the violence of a tyrant.
G1332.portee: This word makes concrete the horror of the massacre of the Innocents: these are not abstractions, but young children, little ones who have just been born or have barely crossed their first birthdays. It confronts us with the brutality with which Herod sought to annihilate the perceived threat to his throne. This passage also reveals how Jesus escaped danger and had to flee to Egypt, highlighting his vulnerability as a child and the divine protection over his life.

sens: duration of twenty-four months
extended period of waiting or confinement
G1333.detail:
1. The word simply designates a period of two years that passes. In Acts 24:27, two years pass while Paul remains in prison under Felix, who hopes to obtain money from him; in Acts 28:30, Paul stays two whole years in Rome under house arrest, receiving anyone who wants to see him.
2. These two uses mark times of waiting or deprivation: Paul awaits judgment, then awaits the end of his confinement. The word emphasizes how significant this time span is in Paul's history — neither short nor definitive, but long enough to weigh heavily.
G1333.origine: The Greek word comes from the adjective "dietès" ("lasting two years"), formed from "dis" (two) and "etos" (year). It is a transparent compound: literally "two-year." The word is rare in biblical Greek and mainly appears in Luke, who likes to specify durations in his accounts.
G1333.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the book of Acts, both by Luke. In Acts 24:27, it measures the duration Paul spends in prison in Caesarea under Felix, the procurator of Judea. In Acts 28:30, it measures the duration Paul spends in Rome, awaiting his trial before Caesar. In both cases, Luke specifies that this time has elapsed ("elapsed," "remained"), giving the narrative a chronological framework and showing how God allows his apostle to be detained, but not indefinitely.
G1333.portee: These two occurrences remind the reader that the Christian life involves times of waiting, sometimes difficult, which are not the absence of God but a moment in the divine plan. Paul is not released, but he is not useless: he receives, he speaks, he continues his mission. The Gospel advances even where the Christian is held back.

sens: To present the facts of a story in detail, in order
To make known what one has seen or learned
To describe actions or events
To publish, announce to others
G1334.detail:
1. To recount means to report a complete story, giving details: it is to say things in their order, as they happened. In Mark 5:16, those who saw the demoniac healed recount precisely what happened to him and to the pigs.
2. The word also designates the act of communicating what one has personally experienced: in Luke 8:39, the man whom Jesus healed must recount all that God has done for him, testifying to his lived experience.
3. To recount can also mean to describe the acts and works of someone to make them known: in Acts 9:27, Barnabas recounts to the apostles how Saul saw Jesus and what he then proclaimed.
4. The verb carries the idea of publication, dissemination: in Luke 8:39, this man "published throughout the city" what Jesus had done, not in secret but by recounting it widely.
G1334.origine: The Greek word is composed of "dia" (through, in detail) and "hegeomai" (to lead, guide). The basic image is that of "leading someone through a story," unfolding it point by point. This composition emphasizes the detailed and orderly nature of the account. In Hebrew, it often translates the verb "safar," which means to enumerate, count, recount.
G1334.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts, to report how events are recounted. Mark uses it when the witnesses of the miracle recount the healing of the demoniac (Mark 5:16). Luke uses it for Jesus' command not to say anything before the Resurrection (Mark 9:9) and for the order to recount the benefits received (Luke 8:39, Luke 9:10). In Acts, it is the verb of apostolic testimony: Barnabas recounts to Peter the conversion of Saul (Acts 9:27), and Peter recounts to the mother of John Mark the events of his release (Acts 12:17). In Acts 8:33, in a prophetic citation, it designates the one who "depicts" the offspring of the suffering servant. The verb is always associated with public narrative and testimony.
G1334.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of personal testimony in the Christian faith: recounting what God has done for us is not optional; it is an act of proclaiming his grace. Jesus commands the Gadarene to recount his benefits (Luke 8:39), and the man obeys by publishing everywhere what Jesus has accomplished. The verb invites every believer to become a witness who faithfully and in detail reports what they have experienced from God, so that others may learn and believe.

sens: Account of facts and events, composed and written to transmit memory
Ordered report intended to inform or instruct
G1335.detail:
1. The word designates a narrative in a literary and structured sense: it is a composed narration, not a simple statement of scattered facts. The context of Luke 1:1 illustrates this well: there is an effort to compose a coherent "narrative" of the events in the life of Jesus, in contrast to the fragmentary traditions that circulated orally before. This is why Luke says, "having undertaken to compose a narrative": there is an effort to organize and write.
2. The word also emphasizes the pedagogical intention: a narrative is not just a list; it is a thoughtful exposition meant to make known or memorize. Luke wants Theophilus — his recipient — to "know with certainty the truth" concerning Jesus, hence the necessity of an ordered narrative rather than chaotic information.
G1335.origine: The word comes from the verb "διηγέομαι" (diēgéomai), which literally means "to lead through" or "to expose in detail." The prefix "διά" marks the complete journey, the traversal of the subject from beginning to end. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this same Greek word often translates "סִפּוּר" (sippour, narrative) or terms designating a report or account of events. The central idea is that of a methodical and complete exposition.
G1335.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:1. It is a literary term deliberately chosen by Luke to qualify his undertaking: to compose an "ordered narrative" of the events of Christ, so that Theophilus can verify the solidity of what he has been taught. This unique occurrence underscores the importance that Luke attributes to the structured narration of evangelical facts, distinct from the simple fragmented oral transmission.
G1335.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Gospels are not random collections of anecdotes, but thoughtful narratives composed with intention. Luke asserts from his prologue that he undertakes to order and verify the facts before transmitting them. This invites the believer to trust in the written Gospel, the result of rigorous research, while encouraging them to deepen their knowledge of Jesus through careful rather than superficial reading.

sens: Character of that which lasts without interruption, without end
Eternal duration, total absence of term
In Scripture, quality of that which is never revoked or abolished
G1336.detail:
1. The word describes what is continuous, without break or interruption. It comes from the verb meaning "to carry through," hence the idea of something that traverses all time, uninterrupted. Melchizedek "remains a priest forever" (Hebrews 7:3), meaning that no succession interrupts him: his priesthood never stops.
2. More broadly, it signifies an endless duration, eternity. When Christ "sat down forever at the right hand of God" (Hebrews 10:12), it expresses that his position of power and honor will never have an end.
3. In the biblical context, it especially qualifies what is definitive and inviolable: Jesus' offering has brought "to perfection forever" those who are sanctified (Hebrews 10:14), meaning that his sacrifice produces a result that will never be annulled or weakened.
G1336.origine: The word is composed of prepositions and the verb meaning "to carry" or "to traverse." Its basic image is that of something that traverses duration without stopping. This term is very rare in Scripture and carries a marked sense of eternity and immutability, particularly suited to the theological language of the New Testament to speak of the timeless nature of God and the action of Christ.
G1336.emploi: The word appears only four times in Hebrews, all in the same theological context: the superiority of Christ and his work. In Hebrews 7:3, it describes the priesthood of Melchizedek which has no end. Then three times in Hebrews 10, it affirms the definitive efficacy of Christ's sacrifice: in 10:1, it contrasts with the "perpetually" repeated Levitical sacrifices and thus ineffective; in 10:12 and 10:14, it proclaims that Christ has offered a single sacrifice "forever" with an eternal and perfect effect. It is a key term to establish that the New Covenant replaces the Old.
G1336.portee: This word invites the believer to place their trust in the completed work of Christ, definitive and unshakeable. Unlike the sacrifices of the Old Covenant that had to be repeated without ever achieving finality, Jesus' sacrifice is unique and produces a perfection that lasts "forever." It is a powerful encouragement for those who doubt: redemption is not fragile or provisional; it is eternal.

sens: Narrow strip of land separating two seas or two bodies of water
Sandbank or reef extending into the sea
G1337.detail: 1. The word describes a strip or tongue of land that divides two bodies of water, or that extends between them. This is the case of a peninsula or a coastal area where land extends into the sea. 2. More concretely, it designates a sandbank, a shoal, or a reef that extends into the water and can run aground a ship. In Acts 27:41, Paul and his companions encounter a "landmass": the ship runs aground on this bank, the bow sinks and gets stuck while the stern breaks under the waves.
G1337.origine: The Greek word δ (dithalassos) is formed from two elements: "dis" (two) and "thalassa" (sea).
