The basic image is therefore literally "two seas" — a place where two bodies of water meet or are divided. This compound describes concrete geographical locations where land interposes between two waters.
G1337.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:41, during the shipwreck of the vessel carrying Paul to Rome. Luke uses this precise term to describe the bank or landmass on which the ship runs aground, probably near the island of Malta. The context shows that it is a geographical formation dangerous for navigation: the ship becomes immobilized and breaks apart.
G1337.portee: This passage reminds us that God controls the forces of nature and remains with his servants in the midst of danger. The shipwreck is not a punishment for Paul, but an opportunity to manifest divine protection and fulfill God's purpose. For the Christian reader, this invites trust in God even when circumstances seem desperate.

sens: That which passes through, that which goes through
That which sinks deeply
That which reaches the most secret or intimate parts
G1338.detail: 1. The verb first designates the physical action of passing through something, of going through: it is the idea of the Greek "dia" (through) and the root meaning to go. 2. Figuratively, it expresses a deep penetration, a capacity to reach what is hidden or distant. In Hebrews 4:12, the word of God is described as "penetrating to the dividing of soul and spirit, joints and marrow": it passes through appearances, it goes beyond what is visible, it reaches the deepest realities of the human being. It is a rare word in biblical Greek, which magnifies the power and sovereign effectiveness of the divine word.
G1338.origine: The word comes from the prefix "dia" (through, by) combined with a root meaning to go or walk. It is a compound verb, formed to express the idea of passing through something. The Greek Old Testament uses it to translate a Hebrew verb meaning to flee or escape (Exodus 26:28), but in Hebrews 4:12, it takes on its full figurative force: penetrating hearts.
G1338.emploi: The word appears only once in the entire New Testament, in Hebrews 4:12. It is chosen to characterize the word of God: not only is it living and effective, not only is it sharper than a sword, but it is also "penetrating." This uniqueness shows the particular importance of this word to describe an essential property of the divine word: its ability to reach what no human discernment can reach alone, to judge the secret feelings and thoughts of the heart. It is a carefully chosen word to express a major spiritual reality.
G1338.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that no secret thought, no hidden intention escapes God who speaks to us through his word. It is both an exhortation to inner honesty and a reason for trust: God knows and judges justly what is hidden in our hearts. The word of God is not superficial; it touches the very roots of our being and brings about a deep transformation.

sens: To stand at a distance, to move away physically
To create an interval, a break between two things or two moments
To diverge, to withdraw
G1339.detail:
1. The primary meaning is spatial: to physically separate from a person or place. When Jesus "separated" from his disciples (Luke 24:51), he moved away from them before being taken up to heaven — a movement of distancing.
2. The word also denotes the idea of an interval that is established: in Luke, there is mention of "an hour" that has elapsed between two moments (Luke 22:59), or the sounding line that measures distance by casting a line into the water (Acts 27:28: the sounding line is cast, then a few fathoms later, it is cast again).
3. More broadly, the word expresses rupture or withdrawal: there is a distance that appears, interposing between what was united.
G1339.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "dia-" (through, between) and "histèmi" (to place, to establish). It literally means "to place a distance" or "to place between." The image is that of something that establishes itself as a separation, a gap. In ancient Hebrew, the Old Testament uses similar words to express the idea of dividing ("chalaq") or separating ("parad").
G1339.emploi: The verb "diistèmi" appears only three times in the New Testament according to the provided usages. In Luke 24:51, it describes the moment when Jesus physically separates from his disciples — a visible moment of rupture before the ascension to heaven. In Luke 22:59, it refers to a lapse of time (about an hour) that has passed. In Acts 27:28, it denotes a marine distance: the sounding line measures depth at two separated points. The word thus encompasses both spatial and temporal separations.
G1339.portee: For a Christian, this word resonates with the experience of presence and absence. The Ascension of Jesus is not an arbitrary disappearance: it is a real and necessary separation that opens the time of the Church, where the disciples must learn to believe without sight. This verb also reminds us that God structures time and space for our good, and that distances do not break the covenant.

sens: To affirm something with strength and assurance, returning to the charge
To firmly support something, without doubt
G1340.detail:
1. To insist means to affirm something by emphasizing it, with conviction and persistence. When the disciples claim that Peter did not deny Jesus, a servant "insists" by saying that this man was surely with him (Luke 22:59): he returns to the charge, affirming the same thing with strength.
2. It also means to affirm something with assurance, without wavering. When Rhoda tells her companions that Peter is at the door, she does so without hesitation, firmly: she is sure of what she has heard (Acts 12:15). It is the certainty of an unwavering conviction.
G1340.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means "to lean strongly." It is composed of the prefix "dia" (through) and the verb "iskhurizo" (to strengthen), which itself comes from "iskhus" (strength). The basic idea is one of strength: one affirms something by putting all one's strength and assurance into it. That is why the word translates as "to insist" or "to affirm strongly." A word from the same Greek family, "ischuro" (strong), is found in the Gospel when speaking of a man's strength.
G1340.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 22:59, it describes how a servant returns to the charge and reaffirms that this man (Jesus) was with Peter; the context shows that this is a repeated and emphasized affirmation. In Acts 12:15, Rhoda asserts to her companions that she indeed heard Peter at the door, despite their disbelief. In both cases, the word evokes an affirmation that the speaker does not deny, which he supports with strength. It is a verb that paints the assurance and firmness of tone.
G1340.portee: This word shows us how people react in the face of truth: some insist without a valid reason (the servant affirms based on a mere resemblance), while Rhoda asserts what she has truly observed. For the Christian, it is a lesson: affirming matters of faith requires not only conviction but also being grounded in what one has truly heard or known of Christ.

sens: judgment in accordance with divine justice
fair and blameless verdict
moral discernment rectified by the wisdom of God
G1341.detail:
1. Just judgment is primarily a sentence that corresponds to God's justice: no partiality, no error, no unjust severity. It is the verdict that only God can pronounce with certainty and authority. In Romans 2:5, Paul speaks of the day when God will reveal his just judgment — a judgment based on moral perfection and total knowledge of each person's actions.
2. It also refers to an equitable judgment among men when they imitate divine justice: a verdict rendered without passion, without corruption, giving each what is truly due to them. In John 7:24, Jesus urges to make a just judgment, not relying solely on appearances but discerning the underlying truth.
3. Finally, it is the right moral discernment, the ability to distinguish good from evil with righteousness — not by the flesh or human opinions, but according to God's immutable criteria.
G1341.origine: The Greek word combines two roots: *dike* (justice, right) and *krisis* (judgment, discernment, the act of judging). It is a compound that denotes the judgment that emanates from justice, or that is in accordance with it. This expression speaks of divine justice, which is perfect, without error, and eternal — the justice from which all true human judgment should draw inspiration.
G1341.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament in Greek (Romans 2:5), but the idea of God's just judgment permeates the entire Pauline and Johannine corpus. In Romans 2:5, Paul warns that the hardening of the human heart leads to the accumulation of a reserve of wrath awaiting the day when the full justice of divine judgment will be revealed. This revelation will be impartial and definitive. The expression also appears in John (7:24) with the verb to judge: Jesus calls for a just judgment that rejects the superficial.
G1341.portee: For the believer, meditating on God's just judgment should evoke both fear and trust: fear of the hardening of the heart that accumulates wrath, trust that God will judge with perfect equity, better than any human court. It also invites one to cultivate a right judgment, not partial, that looks to the heart and not just to appearances — a thoughtful justice that honors divine wisdom.

sens: In accordance with God's will and standard
Innocent, without guilt
Fair, giving each what is due
Virtuous, living in accordance with God
Faithful to obligations toward God and neighbor
Morally upright, free from malice
G1342.detail: 1. The word primarily designates one who lives according to the divine standard of justice: it is a conformity with God's will and law. God Himself is just (Romans 3:26), and Christ is just by perfectly fulfilling the Father's will (1 Peter 3:18). 2. Innocent means here free from guilt or fault: Pilate declares just the one who stands before him (Luke 23:47), with no reproach to address. 3. Fair means giving each what is due: a master must grant his servants what is just and fair (Colossians 4:1), that is, their due. 4. Virtuous characterizes the pious person who fears God and obeys Him, like Zechariah and Elizabeth who walked in all the commandments of the Lord (Luke 1:6). 5. Faithful to obligations concerns duties toward God and neighbor: honoring one's parents is just (Ephesians 6:1), obeying authority is just (Acts 4:19). 6. Morally upright is opposed to evil, to the wicked: just works are opposed to evil works (1 John 3:12).
G1342.origine: The Greek word dikaios comes from dikè, which primarily means custom, rule, established order, then right and justice. In biblical Hebrew, it mainly translates tsaddiq, which designates one who is in conformity with God's covenant and law. The word carries the idea of correspondence, of adequacy with a just order that comes from God and not from men.
G1342.emploi: The word is very frequent in the New Testament (76 occurrences). It primarily qualifies persons: God, Christ, and believers who live according to His law. Joseph is called just because he refuses to defame Mary (Matthew 1:19). John the Baptist is a just man observing God's commandments (Mark 6:20). Zechariah and Elizabeth are just, walking in the ways of the Lord (Luke 1:6). But the word also applies to things: the law is just (Romans 7:12), an action, a word, or a judgment can be just. Paul uses the term to say that the one who lives by faith is just before God (Romans 1:17), echoing the prophet Habakkuk. Finally, in apocalyptic literature, the just are those who will inherit eternal life (Matthew 25:46).
G1342.portee: This word is at the heart of the Christian faith: it expresses what pleases God and what is our vocation. Understanding that only Christ is fully just, and that we are justified by Him and not by our works, is liberating. But it also requires that we aspire to live justly, that is, in accordance with the revealed divine will. It is a call to moral and spiritual integrity.

sens: Conformity of life and thoughts to God's will
State of one who is in good standing with God, declared just by Him
Moral virtue: honesty, fairness, kindness in relationships
Fair judgment, condemnation of evil and reward of good
G1343.detail:
1. Justice is primarily the correspondence between our actions, our words, and God's will. It is to accomplish what is just, as Jesus does by being baptized: "it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness" (Matthew 3:15). It is to lead a righteous life in thought and action, which produces holiness (Ephesians 4:24).

2. But the Bible also speaks of a justice that is given to us, imputed: that which God grants us when we believe in Him. This is the heart of Paul's message: "For with the heart one believes and is justified" (Romans 10:10). This justice comes from faith, not from our efforts to uphold the Law (Romans 4:3). It places us in good standing with God.

3. Justice also includes moral goodness toward others: fairness, honesty, generosity. This is why we can speak of works of justice, servants of justice, and the fruit of the Spirit produces "justice and holiness that produce truth" (Ephesians 4:24).

4. Finally, it is God's own attribute when He judges: God is the "just judge" who condemns evil (Acts 17:31) and will establish the final order of the world.
G1343.origine: The Greek word δικαιοσύνη comes from δίκαιος ("just"), which expresses conformity to divine justice. In Hebrew, it primarily translates צֶדֶק ("justice", "righteousness"), justice as moral integrity and conformity to God's will. The notion is deeply theological: biblical justice is not primarily a philosophical virtue, but the right relationship with God and the image of His own justice. The Greek Old Testament uses this word to describe Abraham's integrity and God's faithfulness to His promises.
G1343.emploi: This word is very frequent in the New Testament, especially in Paul (Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, Titus). Paul uses it in two complementary ways: the justice that God grants us by faith (Romans 1:17, 4:3), and the justice that we practice as disciples (Matthew 5:6, 6:1). He opposes it to sin and iniquity (Romans 8:10), emphasizing that it is a gift from Christ, not an accomplishment of the Law (Romans 10:3-5). Peter and James use it to exhort to a righteous life (1 Peter 2:24, James 2:23). Revelation celebrates it as a divine attribute (19:11). Justice toward God and toward neighbor forms a harmonious whole in biblical thought.
G1343.portee: For the believer, justice is both a gift and a duty. It is the foundation of the relationship with God: we are justified by faith, declared just despite our weaknesses. But this justification compels us to seek justice in our actions (Matthew 5:6, 6:33). It gives meaning to moral life: not to earn salvation, but to respond with gratitude to the grace received. Finally, it places the Christian's hope in God's final judgment, which will establish perfect and just justice.

sens: To show, prove that someone or something is right, in their actions or nature
To declare someone righteous, without guilt, before a court or judge
To accept, recognize as legitimate the words or conduct of someone
To establish a person in a right relationship with God, by removing their guilt
G1344.detail:
1. To show or prove that something or someone is right, that their actions conform to justice. In Matthew 11:19, "wisdom is justified by her works": wisdom is recognized as true and founded by the result it produces.
2. To declare someone righteous before the law or a judge, to grant them reason against the accusation. This evokes the courtroom: the judge pronounces the verdict that acquits the accused. In Romans 3:20, "no one will be justified in his sight by the works of the law" — God will not pronounce innocence based on our acts of piety.
3. To give credit, to recognize the legitimacy of what someone says or does. In Luke 16:15, the Pharisees "seek to appear righteous before men": they want to be recognized as good and correct in the eyes of others.
4. In particular, to establish or restore a person in a right relationship with God, by removing their condemnation and guilt. This is the dominant meaning in Romans 8:30: "Those whom he justified, he also glorified" — God declares believers innocent and acceptable, and prepares them for eternal glory.
G1344.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "righteous" (δίκαιος). Adding the suffix "-ōō" means "to make righteous, to declare righteous." In the background, there is the idea of justice, fairness, right: this is why the word naturally evokes the courtroom, where the judge pronounces what is due, what is correct. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb primarily translates the Hebrew word "tsadaqu" which means "to be righteous, to be right" or "to be put forward as righteous." This Hebrew root initially carried the idea of conformity to a standard or a covenant with God.
G1344.emploi: The verb "justify" appears 34 times in the New Testament (the Gospels, Paul, James). In the Gospels (Matthew, Luke), it often means "to show that one is right" or "to recognize as righteous": wisdom is justified by her works (Matthew 11:19), the tax collector leaves the temple justified, that is, recognized as innocent before God (Luke 18:14). In Paul, the word takes on its deepest meaning: it is the action by which God declares the believer righteous and accepted, not by virtue of the Law (Romans 3:20), but through faith in Christ (Romans 3:24-26, Galatians 2:16). Paul emphasizes that this justification comes by faith, not by works (Romans 4:2-5). James uses the verb in a way that seems different: the believer is "justified by works" (James 2:21-25), which means that their living faith is manifested and proven by their actions; far from contradicting Paul, this indicates that true faith, the one that justifies, cannot remain inactive.
G1344.portee: For the Christian, "justify" is the key word of the entire Gospel. It expresses the central good news: God does not judge us based on our performance or moral efforts, but declares us acceptable in Christ through faith. This word reminds us that the relationship with God does not rest on our merits, but on His judgment of mercy toward the one who believes. It is the foundation of the believer's peace: I can know that I am "justified", that is, my case is won before God, because Christ has resolved the problem of sin.

sens: prescription or law established by an authority
judgment or decision of a court
act of justice or work conforming to justice
G1345.detail:
1. An ordinance is a rule, a command established to be observed: it is a law or an official prescription. In Luke 1:6, Zechariah and Elizabeth observed "all the ordinances of the Lord", that is, all the commandments and rules that God had set in the Law.

2. An ordinance can also refer to a judgment rendered by a court, especially a decision of condemnation or acquittal. In Romans 1:32, the "judgment of God" is His sentence against sin; in Romans 5:16, the ordinance can be either a condemnation or a justification (acquittal).

3. More broadly, an ordinance is an act of justice, a just work accomplished. In Romans 5:18, "one act of righteousness" by Christ brings justification to all men: it is His just and saving work that unfolds for all.
G1345.origine: The word comes from the verb "justify" (δικαιόω), which means to declare or recognize someone as righteous. An ordinance is therefore what results from this declaration of justice: it is the concrete expression of justice, either in the form of a rule to follow, or in the form of a judgment rendered, or in the form of a just act accomplished. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word חֹק (houq, "law", "decree").
G1345.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, especially in Paul (Romans and Hebrews). In Luke and Romans 2, it refers to the commandments and rules of the Law to be observed. In Romans 5, it takes on a more theological meaning: it designates the judgment of God (condemnation or justification) or the act of justice of Christ. In Hebrews 9, it refers to the cultic ordinances of the tabernacle, the rites to be performed. In Revelation 15 and 19, it refers to the just works of believers. The meaning thus oscillates between rule, judgment, and just act, but all uses emphasize something that manifests or expresses justice.
G1345.portee: This word reminds the Christian that justice is not an abstraction: it is expressed in commandments to observe, in judgments rendered, in concrete acts. This is particularly strong in Romans 5:18, where the unique act of justice of Christ saves all men. This shows that salvation is not simply a word or a declaration, but the effect of a just and perfect work accomplished once for all.

sens: In a just manner, conforming to moral righteousness and the law of God
In an equitable manner, giving each what they deserve
In a suitable manner, appropriate to the situation
With wisdom and righteousness in conduct
G1346.detail:
1. To act justly is to act in accordance with God's justice. Jesus entrusted himself to the one who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23), that is, to the Father who pronounces a right and moral judgment.
2. It is also to give to each according to their deeds: on the cross, the criminal acknowledges that he and his companion are receiving justly what their crimes deserve, while Jesus has done nothing wrong (Luke 23:41).
3. To live justly means to conduct oneself in a suitable and holy manner: Paul praises the Thessalonians for their holy, just, and blameless life (1 Thessalonians 2:10), and the apostle calls to return to oneself as is suitable (1 Corinthians 15:34).
4. It is also to follow wisdom by renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires to live with justice and piety (Titus 2:12).
G1346.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective δίκαιος (dikaios), which means "just." It expresses the idea of moral and legal righteousness, of conformity to the order established by divine justice. The Greek δικαίως translates the Hebrew צֶדֶק (tsedeq) and its derivatives in the Old Testament, words that evoke rectitude, righteousness, and justice established by God Himself.
G1346.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, in contexts that emphasize moral righteousness and just judgment. In Luke 23:41, it expresses the fairness of the deserved punishment. In 1 Corinthians 15:34, it characterizes a suitable and sober conduct. In 1 Thessalonians 2:10, it describes a holy and blameless life. In Titus 2:12, it is part of essential Christian values: wisdom, justice, and piety. In 1 Peter 2:23, it qualifies God's own judgment, which judges with perfect righteousness. The adverb thus covers both just human action and perfectly equitable divine action.
G1346.portee: This word reminds the Christian that justice is not a matter of opinion or feelings, but of conformity to the moral order established by God. It invites one to conduct their life with righteousness, knowing that God judges justly and gives to each according to their works. It is also a source of peace: by entrusting our disputes to the one who judges justly, as Jesus did, we find rest and confidence in divine wisdom.

sens: The action of declaring someone righteous before God
The act by which God acquits the guilty and restores them to righteousness
The result of this declaration: the state of the one who is justified
G1347.detail:
1. It is the action itself, the act of declaring someone righteous. God does not simply say, "you are righteous" — He acts to make you righteous before Him, freeing you from the guilt of your sins. In Romans 4:25, it is Jesus who "was raised for our justification": His resurrection is the act that makes us righteous.
2. More specifically, it is the acquittal: God "acquits" us of our offenses, like a judge who pronounces a verdict of not guilty in court. But this is not a mere fiction — it is a real act that restores us to righteousness and reconciles us with God.
3. Finally, the word also refers to the result, the lasting effect of this act: the "justification that brings life" (Romans 5:18), that is, the state of the one who remains acquitted and alive in God, restored to a right relationship with Him.
G1347.origine: The word comes from the verb δικαιόω (dikaioô), "to make righteous, to declare righteous." It is formed from δίκαιος (dikiaios), "righteous, in accordance with justice." In Hebrew, this group of words often translates מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat), which speaks of judgment, law, and righteousness. The initial image is that of the courtroom: it is the act of the judge pronouncing a sentence of justice.
G1347.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul’s letter to the Romans, which deeply addresses salvation and man's relationship to God. In Romans 4:25, Paul states that Jesus "was raised for our justification," linking the act of justification to the resurrection of Christ. In Romans 5:18, he contrasts the "condemnation" that comes from Adam with the "justification that brings life" that comes from Jesus, showing that it is through this act of justification that life and divine grace reach all men. The context is always that of salvation: how man, guilty and sinful, becomes righteous in the eyes of God.
G1347.portee: This word is at the heart of the Gospel: it concretely explains what it means to be saved. It is not a mere excuse or vague forgiveness — it is a legal act where God declares you righteous and restores your relationship with Him. Understanding justification allows the Christian to grasp why Jesus died and rose again, and what His death and resurrection accomplish for him personally. It is the foundation of the certainty of salvation: you are not justified by your works, but by the grace of God in Jesus Christ.

sens: one who administers justice by examining a case
one who resolves a dispute between two people
one who has the authority to condemn or acquit
one who evaluates and decides
G1348.detail:
1. The judge is primarily the one who presides over a trial: he examines the facts, listens to the parties, and renders a decision. In Acts 7:27 and 7:35, Moses is called "leader and judge" by the Hebrew people in Egypt — that is, he is recognized as having the authority to resolve conflicts among them.
2. This word more broadly designates one who holds the power to settle a dispute, to arbitrate between people. It carries the idea of recognized judicial authority.
3. In a figurative sense, it is one who evaluates, who discerns right from wrong, the just from the unjust — one before whom to give an account.
G1348.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb dikázō (to judge, to administer justice). In ancient Attica, the dikastai were the jurors who composed a court, distinct from the kritès who presided. The term emphasizes the act of judgment itself. In biblical Hebrew, it often translates shophat (שָׁפַט), which means to judge, to govern — a rich word since the ancient judges of Israel (Gideon, Deborah) both governed and administered justice.
G1348.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 7:27-35, in Stephen's speech. There, he uses the word to remind how the people of Israel once recognized Moses as a judge — one who was to govern them and arbitrate their disputes. It is a more formal and legal term than "critic" (kritès): it emphasizes the precise judicial function, not just judgment in general. Luke chooses this word to show the institutional authority that Moses received from God.
G1348.portee: This word reminds us that judgment is a sacred function: the one who judges acts with the authority of God. For the Christian, it raises the question of who we recognize as arbiter — and who will ultimately judge our actions. This prepares the declaration of Jesus that the Father has entrusted all judgment to the Son (John 5:22).

sens: The right, what is just and legal
A court decision, a judgment
The punishment or condemnation that results from it
Justice personified, as a power that executes divine vengeance
G1349.detail:
1. The word δίκη primarily refers to the right, the just rule that governs relationships between men. It is the established order, what is legal and fair.

2. It can mean a legal action, a trial, or the decision rendered by the court: the judgment itself. The Greeks and Romans were well acquainted with this judicial term.

3. The most common meaning in the New Testament is the punishment or penalty inflicted on one who has committed a wrongful act. In 2 Thessalonians 1:9, "to suffer justice" means to undergo divine punishment. Similarly, in Jude 7, the inhabitants of Sodom "suffer" the judgment of eternal fire: it is the execution of the sentence.

4. Sometimes, justice is personified as a divine power that avenges crimes, like a goddess. In Acts 28:4, after Paul is bitten by a snake and does not die, the inhabitants of Malta see there the action of "Justice": an invisible power that strikes the guilty.
G1349.origine: The word δίκη comes from a very ancient Greek root denoting the just order of things. It has given rise in Greek to words of the same family: δικαιός (just), δικαιοσύνη (justice), δικάζω (to judge). In Hebrew, it often translates נָקָם (vengeance) or רִיב (trial, dispute), showing that for the ancients, justice and vengeance against evil went hand in hand.
G1349.emploi: The word δίκη appears only three times in the New Testament. In Acts 28:4, it refers to divine justice as a power that executes vengeance on the guilty. In 2 Thessalonians 1:9, "to suffer justice" refers to the eternal punishment that the unbelievers will endure on the day of judgment. In Jude 7, it signifies the penalty or judgment that strikes Sodom and Gomorrah. In all cases, δίκη speaks less of the virtue of justice than of its execution: the punishment, the retribution for evil.
G1349.portee: This word reminds the reader that divine justice is not abstract: it executes, it strikes, it punishes. God does not leave evil unpunished. But it also invites us not to flee from justice, for for the one who repents and believes, it is Christ who has suffered justice in our place.

sens: Fishing gear made of mesh to catch fish
Hunting or war instrument to trap or hold
G1350.detail: 1. The net is a fishing device made of ropes or threads woven into mesh, thrown or submerged in water to catch fish. It is the primary tool of fishermen on the Sea of Galilee during the time of Jesus: the disciples Simon, James, and John are all fishermen who regularly cast and repair their nets (Matthew 4:20-21, Luke 5:2, 4). This word refers to both the net that is thrown and pulled back as well as the gear maintained at rest. 2. By extension, the net can refer to any trapping device that is stretched or thrown to ensnare, whether in hunting or even in warfare. The image of the net also symbolizes imprisonment or the inevitable danger tightening around someone.
G1350.origine: The Greek word δίκτυον comes from an ancient root related to the idea of weaving or interlacing meshes. In Hebrew, it primarily translates to רֶשֶׁת and שְׂבָכָה, both terms for the nets of fishermen or the snares of a hunter. The word evokes the action of stretching, interlacing, creating a meshed surface capable of holding. It is a very concrete term, tied to the trades of fishing and hunting in the ancient Near East.
G1350.emploi: This word appears about a dozen times in the New Testament, concentrated in the accounts of the calling of the first disciples (Matthew 4, Mark 1, Luke 5) and in the account of the miraculous catch after the Resurrection (John 21). The usage is exclusively literal and concrete: never figurative in the New Testament, the net remains the working instrument of fishermen. The synoptics mention it when Jesus calls the disciples from the Sea of Galilee: they literally leave their nets to follow him (Matthew 4:20, Mark 1:18). In John 21, the disciples cast the net after the Resurrection and bring it back full of fish, an image of abundant gathering. No major nuance: the word retains its technical and material meaning everywhere.
G1350.portee: For the Christian, the net evokes the humble and patient work of the first disciples before their transformation into fishers of men. Seeing Jesus call Simon, James, and John at the moment they are mending or casting their nets reminds us that God's call interrupts ordinary work and demands total abandonment. The miraculous catch in chapter 21 of John, where the net overflows with fish, symbolizes the abundant harvest that Jesus promises to those who follow him. It is an image of spiritual fertility and trust in the word of the Lord.

sens: Who speaks with two tongues, who says one thing and its opposite
Who lacks sincerity, who is hypocritical or dishonest in their words
G1351.detail:
1. The word paints the image of a person who speaks with "two tongues" — they say one thing to one person and the opposite to another, or they say one thing in public and contradict it in private. It is someone who does not have a stable and reliable word.
2. By extension, it describes moral hypocrisy: one who is not sincere, who hides their true intentions, who seeks to deceive. In 1 Timothy 3:8, Paul asks that deacons not be "double-tongued" — meaning they must be men of single word, honest and trustworthy in all they say.
G1351.origine: The word comes from the root "di-" (two) and "logos" (word, tongue). The image is of a person who possesses two tongues and uses them to deceive. A similar idea is found in "diglôsse" (two tongues), which in ancient Greek refers to one who speaks two different languages, but here the moral sense prevails: two tongues in one mouth, which do not say the same thing.
G1351.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 3:8, where Paul lists the moral qualities required of deacons. It is part of a list of vices to avoid — drunkenness, financial dishonesty — and emphasizes that service in the Church requires integrity of speech. The absence of other occurrences shows that this technical term describes a specific and serious moral flaw: the unfaithfulness of the tongue.
G1351.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us of the importance of sincerity and honesty in speech. It calls for speaking the truth without calculation, not adapting one's discourse according to current interests. Especially for those who hold responsibility in the Church, "double tongue" is a poison: it destroys trust and renders any ministry ineffective.

sens: For this reason, because of this
Consequently, as a result of what has just been said
It is necessary, one must (sense of exhortation or conclusion)
G1352.detail:
1. The word expresses a logical consequence: it shows that what follows directly stems from what precedes. When Matthew writes, "Therefore this field has been called the field of blood" (Matthew 27:8), he explains that the name of the field comes from the act that has just been recounted. It is the clearest link of cause and effect.
2. Sometimes it introduces a conclusion or an exhortation that is imperative: "Therefore, come out from among them" (2 Corinthians 6:17) means that the command to separate logically follows from what has been taught before. It urges the reader to act or think in a certain way.
3. In other contexts, especially when reinforced by other words ("therefore also", "for this reason"), it marks the fulfillment of a promise or the conclusion of a reasoning: in Hebrews 11:12, "therefore" introduces the consequence of Abraham's faith.
G1352.origine: The word comes from the contraction δι᾽ ὅ ("for this" or "by this"). Δι-ὅ literally meant "by which" or "because of which". It is a linking particle that combines two ideas: "because of" and "therefore". It is found in the Pauline epistles notably, where it structures theological argumentation.
G1352.emploi: This word occurs 52 times in the New Testament, especially in the epistles. Paul uses it abundantly to chain his theological ideas: in Romans 1:24, he explains the consequences of rejecting God with a "therefore" that introduces divine abandonment. The Gospels use it to link events: Matthew recounts a fact, then "therefore" draws the conclusion or explains the name. Hebrews often uses it to apply the Old Testament to the believer's life: in Hebrews 13:12, "therefore" shows how Jesus' offering should modify our attitude. The context varies: sometimes it is a simple causality ("because this, therefore that"), sometimes an exhortation ("since it is so, act"), sometimes the fulfillment of a promise.
G1352.portee: This small word helps the believer see the logic of God's will. When Paul writes "Therefore", he shows that the Christian life is not a series of arbitrary commands, but the just and good consequence of revealed truth. Understanding these connections "why → therefore" leads to thinking as the Bible thinks: not juxtaposing ideas, but seeing how faith and life logically connect.

sens: to travel through a country, a region, moving from one place to another
to cross a space, to pass through places
G1353.detail:
1. The word describes the action of traveling through a region: one does not stop in a single place, but goes from town to town or from village to village. This is what Jesus does in Luke 8:1 when he "went" to proclaim the Gospel, traveling through the towns and villages of Galilee, like a prophet moving to fulfill his mission.
2. It can also refer to the simple act of crossing a space or passing through places without necessarily stopping for long. This is the case in Acts 17:1: Paul and Silas "passed" through two cities (Amphipolis and Apollonia) to reach Thessalonica, which was their true destination.
G1353.origine: The word is composed of "dia" (through) and "odeuo" (to travel, to go on the way, from "hodos": the road). The basic image is that of movement through a space, following the paths. It is a verb of movement that emphasizes the passage from one place to another, rather than a simple stationary presence.
G1353.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament according to the Segond. In the Gospel of Luke (8:1), it depicts Jesus on a traveling mission, traversing the regions to preach. In Acts (17:1), it describes Paul's missionary journey, who crosses certain cities to reach others. The word always applies to journeys that involve multiple stages or passages, never to a simple movement within a single place.
G1353.portee: This verb reminds us that the minister of Christ is often a work of movement and passage: it is about not remaining static, but going to the people. Jesus himself "went" from town to village to proclaim the Gospel, and Paul follows the same model. For the Christian, it is a subtle call not to confine one's faith to a single place or community, but to carry it where God calls them.

sens: Athenian who converted to faith in Jesus Christ upon hearing the apostle Paul
G1354.detail: Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus, the council that governed Athens — indicating his high status in the city. When Paul preached in Athens, presenting the Gospel before this same council, some listeners attached themselves to him and believed, among whom was Dionysius (Acts 17:34). He represents a rare example of conversion among the Athenian elite, showing that the Gospel transcends social and intellectual barriers.
G1354.origine: The name Dionysius (Greek Dionusios) is derived from the name of the Greek god Dionysus (god of wine and festivity). Although born of a polytheistic culture, Dionysius abandoned his pagan beliefs to embrace Christ.
G1354.emploi: Dionysius appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:34. It is during Paul's speech at the Areopagus, where the apostle addressed the Athenians about their altar "To an unknown god" and announced to them the resurrected Jesus. Dionysius reacted to this message by believing. Ancient traditions held him to be one of the first bishops of Athens, although Scripture itself says nothing more about him.
G1354.portee: Dionysius embodies the universal call of the Gospel: no one is too far away, too wise in their own understanding, or too entrenched in human systems to hear and receive the Good News. His example encourages the reader to believe that Christ can transform even those who seem the most improbable or the most rooted in worldly philosophy.

sens: for this specific reason
as a consequence of what has just been said
marks a logical and certain deduction
G1355.detail: 1. It is a conjunction that introduces a strong conclusion: it connects what has just been said to what is deduced from it. In 1 Corinthians 8:13, Paul has just explained that eating may scandalize a weak brother; then he concludes: "Therefore, if food scandalizes my brother, I will never eat meat." The reason is clearly established, and the consequence follows. 2. This conjunction reinforces the idea of cause by adding a nuance of insistence: it is not a simple "therefore," but a "it is very precisely for this reason." In 1 Corinthians 10:14, after reminding that we have broken with idolatry through communion, Paul says: "Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry." The order directly and necessarily follows from what precedes it.
G1355.origine: This Greek word unites two elements: διό ("for which," "therefore") and πέρ (a particle that reinforces and emphasizes). Together, they create a conjunction that is stronger and more emphatic than the simple διό. It is like adding "very" or "precisely" in French to say not only "therefore" but "it is precisely for this reason that."
G1355.emploi: This word appears twice in the New Testament, only in Paul in 1 Corinthians. In both cases, it introduces an ethical or behavioral consequence: not to eat meat if it scandalizes a brother (8:13), and to flee idolatry (10:14). Paul uses it to firmly unite theology (what is true) with action (what must be done). It is a conjunction characteristic of Pauline logic: first the teaching, then the exhortation that follows from it.
G1355.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is never purely theoretical: it must translate into actions. When we understand a biblical truth, the consequence for our life logically follows. Paul uses this conjunction to show that love for one's neighbor and breaking with idolatry are not options, but inevitable deductions from our position in Christ.

sens: That has descended or fallen from heaven
That comes directly from a heavenly or divine source
That has a supernatural origin
G1356.detail:
1. The word literally designates something that has fallen from heaven, come from above. In Acts 19:35, the city clerk of Ephesus speaks of the statue of Diana: according to local belief, this image miraculously reached the earth from heaven, which made it extraordinarily sacred.
2. More broadly, it qualifies what has a supernatural or divine origin, sent by the gods or by God himself. Such provenance confers to the object or phenomenon an undeniable character of authority and holiness.
3. The word implicitly opposes what is made by man: it is the authentic, the true, the divinely attested. The Ephesians invoke this image to defend the worship of Diana against those who questioned it.
G1356.origine: The Greek word is composed of "dio-" (from heaven, from Zeus) and "peptē" (fallen, from "pipeskein" = to fall). This formation literally suggests "fallen from heaven." It is a rare word in ancient Greek, forged to express this specific idea of a cult object reputed to have a celestial origin. The root evokes the image of a miraculous descent.
G1356.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 19:35, during the riot of the silversmiths in Ephesus. The city clerk uses it to calm the crowd by recalling the prestigious local tradition: the image of Diana would have "fallen from heaven." This is a strong argument in ancient culture, where objects of celestial origin enjoyed particular veneration. This unique usage reflects the rhetoric of the opponents of the Gospel, who defended their traditional cults.
G1356.portee: This word reveals how men attribute superhuman authority to objects shaped by man, seeking to legitimize them by claiming them from heaven. For the Christian reader, it is a sober lesson on idolatry: false cults adorn themselves with the prestige of the divine without possessing the reality. Only the Word of God truly has a heavenly provenance and absolute authority.

sens: Action de redresser, de rendre droit
Action de corriger, de refondre
Rénovation ou restauration d'un ordre ancien
G1357.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes the action of straightening or making right — it is the basic concrete image, as one straightens what is bent. 2. It then signifies the correction or reworking of a law, institution, or practice: a renewal, a restoration that improves or refreshes. It is in this sense that it is used in Hebrews 9:10, where the Apostle Paul speaks of a "time of reformation" — the moment when the old carnal ordinances (sacrifices, washings, rules about food) would be corrected or transformed, likely referring to the fulfillment in Christ. 3. More broadly, the word can denote a renovation, a restoration intended to correct the old state or to make it better.
G1357.origine: The word comes from the verb "to straighten, to correct" (διορθόω): it combines two elements — "through" and "right" — which together evoke the idea of making right, of rectifying. This same root can be found in French words like "orthodoxe" (which goes straight). The basic idea is mechanical (straightening a curved line) before becoming moral or institutional (correcting a practice, reworking a law).
G1357.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament: in Acts 24:2-3 and in Hebrews 9:10. In Acts, the related term "correction" (διόρθωμα) refers to the improvements made by Governor Felix to the affairs of Judea — a very concrete sense of administrative management. In Hebrews 9:10, the word takes on an eschatological sense: Paul uses it to refer to the time when the legal ordinances of the Old Testament would be replaced or fulfilled — not abolished, but corrected, brought to their true end in Christ. It is a reformation in the sense of transitioning from the old to the new regime.
G1357.portee: This word reminds us that the laws and institutions of the Old Testament are not arbitrary or definitive, but oriented towards a fulfillment. The notion of reformation invites the Christian to see in Christ not a rejection of the Law, but its realization, its alignment with the right path. It is also an invitation to vigilance: every religious practice must be tested and possibly corrected to remain faithful to the Gospel.

sens: Creuser à travers un mur ou une paroi, en particulier pour forcer l'entrée d'une maison
Dérober en forçant l'entrée
Au sens figuré, atteindre ou détruire par infiltration
G1358.detail:
1. The word describes the action of digging, of piercing a wall or partition to make a hole. It is the act of a thief who digs through the wall of a house to enter: the householder must be vigilant so that the thief does not "pierce" his dwelling (Matthew 24:43).

2. By extension, the verb denotes the action of burglarizing, of stealing by forcing entry: thieves who pierce houses enter to steal the treasures accumulated there (Matthew 6:19).

3. Figuratively, Jesus uses it to speak of what destroys our earthly possessions: moth and rust "pierce" our riches, meaning they slowly eat away at them and destroy them from within (Matthew 6:19-20).
G1358.origine: The Greek verb is composed of the prefix "dia-" (through) and the root "orussô" (to dig, to bore). The starting image is that of digging, boring through a solid material. This verb belongs to the vocabulary of construction and land work: the one who digs crosses the obstacle. The Hebrew root "hâthar" (חָתַר) that expresses it in Exodus 12:5-7 means precisely "to dig, to make a hole, to break."
G1358.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, and always in a context of wealth and security. In Matthew 6:19-20, Jesus uses it twice to warn against the accumulation of earthly treasures: these riches are fragile, threatened by thieves who pierce them. In Matthew 24:43 and Luke 12:39, the verb describes the thief who pierces the master's house, an image that Jesus uses to speak of his unexpected return. The meaning remains constant: an action of breaking, of penetrating by force, whether physical or destructive.
G1358.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on the real value of their possessions. Jesus uses it to show that earthly riches are ephemeral, always threatened by loss or destruction, while heavenly treasures remain inviolable. It is a call to reorient our priorities: to accumulate what wears out and is lost, or to invest in eternity. The word also reminds us that the return of Christ will be sudden and unexpected, like the arrival of a thief in the night.

sens: Les Dioscures
Dieux jumeaux de la mythologie grecque, fils de Zeus et de Léda, nommés Castor et Pollux
G1359.detail: The Dioscures are two twin gods of Greek mythology, presented as the sons of Zeus and the goddess Leda. Their name literally means "sons of Zeus." In legend, Castor and Pollux are among the Argonauts and are honored as protectors of sailors. In Acts 28:11, Paul boards a merchant ship that bears "the Dioscures as its emblem," meaning that a figure or emblem of the twin gods adorned the ship — a common practice among ancient ships that placed themselves under the protection of a deity.
G1359.origine: The Greek word Διόσκουροι is composed of Διός (Dios, genitive of Zeus, the king of the gods) and κόρος (koros, a son or young man). The name thus literally designates "the sons of Zeus." This cult is of Greek origin and spread widely throughout the Mediterranean world, particularly revered by sailors who saw in Castor and Pollux protectors at sea.
G1359.emploi: The Dioscures appear only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:11. Paul and his companions, on their way to Rome as prisoners, board an Alexandrian ship that bore the Dioscures as its emblem. This unique usage illustrates how ancient vessels displayed the symbols of protective deities. For the reader of the New Testament, it is simply a historical detail that shows how navigation and the religious life of pagans functioned at the time.
G1359.portee: The mention of the Dioscures reminds us that Paul traveled in a world saturated with pagan religious practices, where sailors entrusted their safety to other gods. It also highlights the sovereign protection of the God of Israel who accompanies the apostle to Rome, despite storms and dangers, regardless of the emblems that the ships bore.

sens: Conjunction introducing the cause or reason for a statement
Introducing an explanation or justification
Expressing the reason for a command or recommendation
G1360.detail:
1. This word introduces the reason or cause for what has just been said. It answers the question "why?" In Romans 3:20, Paul explains: "No one will be justified before him by the works of the law, for it is through the law that comes the knowledge of sin" — the word "for" shows that it is the function of the law (to make sin known) that prevents justification by it.
2. It can introduce the reason for an emotion or feeling. In Philippians 2:26, Epaphroditus was "deeply distressed because you had heard of his illness" — the word "for" (in the Greek text) explains why he was distressed: because you had heard of his illness.
3. Sometimes it introduces the reason for a command or warning: "Do not defraud your brother, for the Lord will take vengeance on all these things" (1 Thessalonians 4:6). Here the motive for the command is exposed.
G1360.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and is composed of two elements: "dia" (through, by) and "oti" (that, because). Its fundamental meaning refers to "by this that" or "for this that." It is a causal conjunction, meaning it links a cause to its effect or consequence. It is stronger and more explicit than the simple "oti" (that), as it emphasizes the causal link more.
G1360.emploi: This conjunction appears 22 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Pauline epistles (Romans, 1 and 2 Thessalonians, 1 Corinthians, Philippians) and in the Gospels (particularly Luke), as well as in Hebrews, James, and 1 Peter. It is always used to introduce a cause or explanation. Depending on the context, the Segond translates it as "for," "because," "why," "since," or even by an expression like "deeply distressed" when it fits into the French phrasing. Its use shows that the author wants to clarify, justify, or deepen what he has just said. It can introduce the reason for a doctrinal statement (Romans 3:20), an order (1 Thessalonians 4:6), or a feeling (Philippians 2:26).
G1360.portee: This small word helps the reader understand the cause-and-effect links in biblical thought. It shows that the Bible does not merely state truths but grounds them on reasons: God acts and speaks for specific motives, often revealed by this word. Grasping these causal links helps to delve deeper into the logic of Scripture and to see how each commandment or promise is rooted in the nature and plans of God.

sens: man mentioned in the third epistle of John
G1361.detail: Diotrephes is a character that the apostle John mentions only once in the Bible, in his short third letter. John describes him as someone who "loves to be first" among the Christians, refusing to receive John's messengers and even expelling from the assembly those who wanted to welcome them. He is an example of one who places his authority and personal prestige above brotherly reception and communion with the apostles.
G1361.origine: The Greek name Diotrephes is composed of two elements: Dios, which means "of Zeus," and trephès, which means "nourished" or "raised." Together, the name literally evokes "one who is cherished or nourished by Zeus." It was a common Greek name, borne by various personalities in antiquity. In the biblical context, this name has no other significance than to identify this particular Christian.
G1361.emploi: Diotrephes appears only once in the Bible, in 3 John 9. John mentions him to rebuke his attitude: he loves to dominate, refuses to welcome the brothers sent by John, and excommunicates those who would do so. John says he will speak more about him when he sees him in person. This brief but vivid portrait reveals the tensions and conflicts of leadership that existed in the early Christian assemblies of the first century. Diotrephes represents one who succumbs to pride and the desire for power within the community.

sens: which is composed of two equal parts
which is worth twice as much
which is increased, reinforced
G1362.detail:
1. Double: that which consists of two identical or equivalent elements. In 1 Timothy 5:17, the elders deserve "double honor" — not two different types of honor, but an honor that is worth twice that of others, or manifestly reinforced.
2. That which represents a quantity multiplied by two. In Revelation 18:6, Babylon must receive "double according to her works" — that is, a punishment equal to twice what she has poured out, an intensified retribution.
3. By extension, that which is taken to an excessive or doubled degree. In Matthew 23:15, the Pharisees make the proselyte "twice as much" a child of hell — not slightly, but in an accentuated manner, reinforcing his waywardness.
G1362.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to fold" or "to double." The basic image is that of something being folded in half, being doubled. In Hebrew, the Bible uses words from the same family (כָּפַל "kapal," to fold; מִשְׁנֶה "mishné," double, which also suggests repetition) to express this idea of multiplication or duplication. The Greek "diplous" retains this concrete idea: two times the same thing.
G1362.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in contexts of evaluation or retribution. In 1 Timothy 5:17, it qualifies the honor due to faithful elders — a recognition that must be manifest and generous. In Revelation 18:6, it expresses divine justice that gives Babylon "double" what she has committed — a reward or punishment that doubles the initial measure. In Matthew 23:15, the comparative "diplóteron" ("twice as much") accentuates the reproach: the Pharisees aggravate the spiritual corruption of their converts. The word oscillates between a reward (honor), a retribution (punishment), and an aggravation (guilt).
G1362.portee: For the believer, this word reminds that God sees and renders justice accurately — he does not give the simple, but the double if necessary. It also invites to generously honor those who faithfully work for the Gospel, not in a modest measure, but with manifest and renewed esteem.

sens: Render twice as much
Give in compensation double what has been received
Pay the retribution by doubling the measure
G1363.detail:
1. The word expresses the idea of doubling something, multiplying it by two. It is an act of compensation or retribution that brings the measure to double.

2. In the context of Revelation 18:6, it refers to rendering to Babylon double what she has poured out: as she has filled the cup of evil against others, a cup twice as full will be poured out to her in return. This is the principle of amplified divine retribution, where God's justice exceeds simple equivalence to emphasize the gravity of judgment.
G1363.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "diplos" which means "double." It is a verb formed to express the action of doubling, of rendering two times larger. The prefix "di-" indicates the number two, and the root evokes the idea of folding or duplication. It is a particular word in Greek, with no direct Hebrew equivalent, but the idea of double retribution is found in the Old Testament (for example in Jeremiah 16:18, where it speaks of paying double).
G1363.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:6, in the context of the judgment of Babylon. John describes how God will render to the great city double for her offenses. The use is clearly legal and eschatological: it concerns the final divine judgment where the retribution surpasses the initial fault. This rarity of the term underscores its importance: John chooses this precise word to express not only justice (paying according to one's works) but also the amplification of that justice (double).
G1363.portee: This word reminds the reader that God does not leave anything unpunished. Divine retribution is not arbitrary, but it sometimes exceeds simple equality: it can be amplified to manifest the gravity of judgment. This is a motive of hope for the persecuted and a warning for the oppressors. The Christian understands that God keeps his accounts with justice and majesty.

sens: The number two repeated, or two occurrences of the same action
Twice within a given period
Doubling, with intensified intensity
G1364.detail:
1. The word simply means "twice": an action or event that occurs two times. Peter denies Jesus, and Jesus had foretold that before the rooster crows "twice," this would happen (Mark 14:30). The word counts the repetitions.
2. Within a determined timeframe, it indicates frequency or habit: the Pharisee in Luke 18:12 fasts "twice" a week, which was beyond what the Law required. Similarly, Paul states that he received help from the church in Philippi "twice" (Philippians 4:16).
3. Figuratively, "twice" can mean a condemnation or a double state: in Jude 1:12, false teachers are called "twice dead," meaning condemned to spiritual death and destined for destruction, an expression of their desperate state.
G1364.origine: The Greek word δίς comes from the same root as δύο ("two"). It is an adverb simply formed to express repetition: it corresponds to the English "twice." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, a similar expression is found with the repeated number (like "two times two"), but classical Greek uses this simple and clear adverb.
G1364.emploi: The word δίς appears 7 times in the New Testament, primarily in Mark, Luke, and Paul. Mark uses it for the announcement of Peter's denial: the rooster will crow "twice" before Peter denies Jesus (14:30, 14:72). Luke shows its use in a religious context: the Pharisee fasts "twice" a week (18:12). Paul uses it to talk about repeated events: he mentions having been helped "twice" (Philippians 4:16) and having tried to visit the Thessalonians "once and twice" (1 Thessalonians 2:18). In Jude 1:12, it appears in a figurative expression to emphasize double condemnation. Each time, the word simply counts a repetition or emphasizes that an action occurred twice rather than once.
G1364.portee: This small word reminds us of the importance of details in the biblical narrative. The precise mention that the rooster would crow "twice" before Peter's denial shows the knowledge that Jesus had of the future and the certainty of His word. For the Christian reader, this invites trust in the Lord's words even in their concrete details. It is also a word that anchors the Bible in real and historical situations: fasting "twice" a week, helping "twice," shows that faith is expressed in concrete and measurable actions.

sens: To hesitate in the face of a decision or statement, wavering between two positions
To lack confidence in God or in His word
To be unsure of the truth or reality of something
G1365.detail:
1. The word describes the act of hesitating or wavering mentally in the face of something: one does not decide, one wavers. In Matthew 14:31, Peter walks on water toward Jesus but begins to be afraid; Jesus reproaches him for having doubted, meaning he lost his certainty and allowed himself to be troubled by the waves.
2. To doubt also means to lack trust—particularly in God. Jesus calls Peter "you of little faith" at the same moment: to doubt is not to trust in the promise or presence of the One who calls us.
3. The word can also simply mean not being sure of what one sees or hears. In Matthew 28:17, after the resurrection, the disciples see Jesus but "some doubted": they are not certain, they hesitate to believe in this extraordinary sight.
G1365.origine: The word comes from the Greek δίς (dis), which means "twice"—the basic idea is that of someone wavering between two positions, unable to decide. It is like being divided within oneself. This image of wavering or instability is found in several related Greek words that express hesitation or perplexity.
G1365.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in the Gospel of Matthew. In both cases, it describes a spiritual weakness: in Peter, it is the hesitation that arises from fear and weakness of faith in the face of the elements (14:31); in the disciples at the resurrection, it is the uncertainty before an event that surpasses understanding (28:17). In both contexts, doubt represents an obstacle to faith and obedience.
G1365.portee: The word confronts us with a vital question: on whom or what do we base our trust? Peter doubts because he looks at the waves instead of looking at Jesus. For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that faith is not an emotional or sensory certainty—it is a heart's adherence to God despite troubling circumstances. Doubt is not the absence of faith, but the moment when faith wavers; that is why Jesus can address it and call him to hold firm.

sens: A sharp weapon that cuts on both sides of its blade
Figuratively, a word or action that has a double effectiveness or double impact
G1366.detail:
1. The word concretely describes a sword or blade that has a cutting edge on each side, not just one. In Revelation, the sword that comes from the mouth of the risen Christ is described as: "Out of His mouth went a sharp two-edged sword" (Revelation 1:16). This image evokes a formidable weapon, capable of striking with equal power in both directions.
2. Figuratively, the word applies to the word of God, which is "living and powerful, sharper than any two-edged sword" (Hebrews 4:12). This word penetrates to the depths of being—soul, spirit, joints, and marrow—and judges the thoughts of the heart. It thus acts doubly: it penetrates and it judges; it divides the visible from the invisible. The double edge symbolizes this dual action: nothing can resist it.
G1366.origine: The Greek word comes from δίς (dis, "twice") and στόμα (stoma, "mouth"), literally "two mouths." This term originally applied to rivers that split into two branches or to roads that fork. Applied to a sword, it designates a blade that has two "mouths" or two edges, one on each side. The initial image is geographical or natural, but it has taken on a martial significance.
G1366.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, solely in John (Revelation) and in the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews. In Revelation 1:16 and 2:12, it qualifies the sword that comes from the mouth of the risen Christ, symbolizing His judgment and power. In the Epistle to the Hebrews 4:12, it qualifies the word of God, which penetrates deeply within us and judges our hidden thoughts. In all cases, the emphasis is on the formidable effectiveness and penetration of what is described.
G1366.portee: This word reminds us that the word of God is never harmless: it acts powerfully within us, dividing good from evil, truth from falsehood, soul from spirit. It judges justly and leaves nothing hidden. It is an invitation to take seriously the Word we read and to allow ourselves to be transformed by it, rather than treating it as an ordinary word.

sens: The number 2000
G1367.detail: 1. The number two thousand: it is simply the figure 2000, expressing a precise quantity. Mark uses it to describe the number of pigs in the herd that rushed into the sea after Jesus allowed the unclean spirits to enter them (Mark 5:13). This figure emphasizes the magnitude of the catastrophe and shows that the narrator has retained a precise detail of the event.
G1367.origine: The Greek word is composed of "di-" (two) and "chilioi" (thousand), literally forming "two-thousand." It is a simple cardinal number, without particular nuance: it denotes an exact quantity.
G1367.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 5:13, during the episode of the demoniac of Gadara. Jesus allows the demons to enter a herd of pigs; the Gospel specifies that there were about two thousand animals. This concrete detail strengthens the narrative by showing the extent of the destruction and the physical reality of the miracle.
G1367.portee: This number reminds us that the Gospel accounts rely on eyewitnesses capable of reporting precise facts. It also underscores the real power of the spiritual forces at play: two thousand living creatures are affected in an instant. For the reader, this detail anchors the miracle in concrete reality rather than in abstraction.

sens: Pour a liquid through a sieve or strainer to purify it
Meticulously eliminate small impurities by retaining them
Figuratively: to be overly meticulous about small details while neglecting the essential
G1368.detail:
1. The word evokes the action of pouring a liquid (wine, water) through a sieve or fine cloth to purify it and retain impurities. It is a common domestic or artisanal gesture in antiquity, aimed at making the drink clear and consumable.

2. More broadly, it means to retain or eliminate scrupulously small undesirable things — here a gnat, that tiny creature one would seek to remove from a cup. This operation requires attention and meticulousness.

3. In Matthew 23:24, Jesus uses this word figuratively to criticize the religious leaders: they meticulously strain (they rigorously observe the small commandments about purity, the tithes of herbs), but they "swallow the camel" — they commit injustice and neglect mercy. The image becomes one of absurd and hypocritical rigor: examining every drop for a gnat, then swallowing a large beast.
G1368.origine: The Greek word is formed from "dia" (through) and the verb "ulizô" (to sift, to filter). Its basic image is thus that of passing through: to pass a liquid through a filter. This etymology is reflected in the very composition of the word: "dia" suggests crossing, the action "through." The image is concrete and domestic, that of the daily work of purifying drinks.
G1368.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Matthew 23:24, at the heart of the discourse where Jesus denounces the hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees. It is used only in a figurative sense, as a critical image of their legalism. Jesus reproaches these religious leaders for their excessive and misplaced scrupulousness: they observe the most minor prescriptions (tithing dill, cumin, and mint) with an obsessive concern for purity, but they overlook the essential commandments — justice, mercy, faithfulness. The verb "strain" perfectly conveys this nuance: an effort of meticulous filtration, but for the wrong reasons and in the wrong place.
G1368.portee: This word reminds the reader of a deep spiritual temptation: that of cultivating an impeccable external piety — regularity, precise observance of rules — while leaving the heart insensitive to justice and compassion. Jesus invites a hierarchy: what is serious (mercy) should not be sacrificed for what is light (ritual form). For the modern Christian, it is a call to examine one's own priorities and hidden hypocrisies: where do I place my zeal, and do I forget the essential?

sens: Cut into two parts
Separate, create discord
Create a rupture, a disagreement
G1369.detail: 1. The literal meaning of the word is to cut something in two — for example, to separate the parts of a poultry when preparing it (an image that the word carries in the Greek Old Testament). 2. Figuratively, it means to create division or disagreement between people, to separate them through conflict. 3. In Matthew 10:35, Jesus says: "I have come to bring division between a man and his father, between a daughter and her mother, between a daughter-in-law and her mother-in-law" — it is the spiritual rupture that the adherence to the Gospel provokes: some family members will follow Jesus, others will reject him, and this loyalty to Christ will create a separation, an antagonism within the household itself.
G1369.origine: The word comes from the Greek adverb dichá ("in two"), which literally expresses division into two parts. It is a verb formed on this root: it means to make two, to split, to divide. Ancient Greek needed a strong term to express this cleavage, both physical and social or moral. In the Greek Old Testament, this word rendered the concrete image of separation (like the sharing of an offering).
G1369.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 10:35. Jesus uses it to announce that his message will generate division within families: those who believe in him and those who reject him will find themselves separated, in conflict. It is a difficult word, reminding us that the Gospel does not come to bring superficial peace, but it demands a choice that can fragment the closest human bonds. The context shows that Jesus does not seek division for its own sake, but it is the inevitable consequence of loyalty to the Kingdom.
G1369.portee: This word reminds us that following Jesus may require the sacrifice of precious relationships and expose us to misunderstanding or opposition from our own. It invites us to count the cost of discipleship and to recognize that our fidelity to Christ takes precedence over earthly family harmony. It also comforts us: if we suffer from ruptures caused by faith, we know that Jesus spoke of it and understands this tearing.

sens: separation into opposing groups
disunion, break in communion
quarrel, conflict
state of persistent disagreement
G1370.detail:
1. The word literally denotes the act of standing apart, of separating. In the Church, this means that believers no longer form a single united body, but divide into opposing camps (Romans 16:17: "those who cause divisions").
2. It is a break in brotherly communion — not just a temporary disagreement, but a persistent separation that weakens the unity of God's people. It goes beyond mere dispute or quarrel.
3. In context, division arises from pride, personal ambition, and selfishness: it emerges when each person defends their own vision rather than seeking harmony (Galatians 5:20, listed among the works of the flesh alongside jealousy and quarrels).
4. It is a serious sin for Paul, who warns believers to clearly distance themselves from those who intentionally provoke it.
G1370.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "dichostatos" which literally means "to stand in two places" or "to be divided in two." It is formed from "di-" (two) and "stasis" (position, station, the act of standing). The basic image is that of a fracture: moving from unity (all standing together) to division (each standing on their own side). It is a rare word in classical Greek, expressing less a simple quarrel than a structural rupture of unity.
G1370.emploi: Paul uses this word three times in his letters, always to describe a serious problem in the Church. In Romans 16:17, he warns against those who "cause divisions" — it is a voluntary and harmful act. In Galatians 5:20, he lists it among the works of the flesh, alongside jealousy, animosity, and quarrels, showing that division is a symptom of a carnal, not spiritual, life. In 1 Corinthians 3:3, the word does not appear literally, but the context evokes the same reality: believers living according to the flesh divide into opposing factions ("I am of Paul, I am of Apollos"). Division is thus always presented as an ecclesial wound to be fought against and fled from.
G1370.portee: For today's believer, this word reminds us of the serious responsibility to preserve the unity of the Church. Division is not merely a difference of opinion, but a rupture that weakens the common testimony and grieves the Holy Spirit. Paul urges us to identify and avoid those who intentionally foment it — not out of harshness, but out of love for the communion of the body of Christ. It is a constant call to reconciliation and humility.

sens: To cut, divide a body into two or more pieces
By extension, to tear, severely lacerate
Figuratively, to punish with severity and cruelty
G1371.detail: 1. The literal meaning is to cut something in two or to divide it into pieces: this was the fate reserved for certain victims in antiquity. 2. The Bible uses it figuratively to describe a severe and painful punishment: in Matthew 24:51 and Luke 12:46, Jesus says that the master will cut his unfaithful servant "in pieces," an image of total rupture with him and the merciless judgment that awaits. 3. It is not necessarily a physical dismemberment, but the expression of a terrible and definitive punishment, like a tearing of fate.
G1371.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "dicha" (in two) and "temno" (to cut, to slice). It is rarely found in ancient texts. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew verb "natah" in the sense of dismembering a sacrificial animal. It is a word formed on the simple notion of division or severed separation.
G1371.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, always in Matthew and Luke, and always in the mouth of Jesus. In Matthew 24:51, it describes the fate of the wicked servant on the day of judgment, mingled with the hypocrites. In Luke 12:46, the context is identical: the servant who does not watch will be separated from his master and cast out with the unfaithful. Jesus uses this violent image to emphasize the irreversibility and gravity of divine judgment on one who betrays his trust.
G1371.portee: This terrible image reminds Christians that serving the Lord requires vigilance and faithfulness. It is not a threat against the believer in Christ, but a serious warning addressed to anyone who receives a responsibility and neglects it. It invites us to take seriously the expectation of Jesus' return and to remain faithful in trust.

sens: To feel the physiological need to drink
To lack water or drink
To intensely desire something persistently
G1372.detail:
1. To be thirsty is to feel the physical need to drink. It is a sensation that torments the thirsty body. In Matthew 25:37, the righteous ask the Lord when they saw him "thirsty," meaning in a state of lacking water.
2. It can also mean being in a state of suffering due to lack of drink. In John 19:28, Jesus on the cross says, "I thirst," expressing an intense physical reality at the heart of his suffering.
3. Figuratively, to be thirsty denotes an intense and deep desire, like a hunger of the soul. In Matthew 5:6, to be "thirsty for righteousness" means to desire it passionately. Similarly, in John 4:14, whoever believes in Jesus "will never thirst": Christ satisfies the deepest desire of the human heart, that for meaning, life, and lasting satisfaction.
G1372.origine: The word διψάω comes from the root δίψα (dipsa), which denotes physical thirst and sensations of dryness in the body. In Hebrew, the verb צָמֵא (tsama) carries the same concrete and figurative meaning: to feel the absence of water, but also to long for, to desire ardently. The Greek of the New Testament captures this polysemy: the word expresses sometimes the brutal physical need, sometimes the deep spiritual aspiration.
G1372.emploi: The verb to thirst appears 16 times in the provided usages, mainly in the Gospels. In Matthew, it denotes the physical thirst of the hungry and thirsty that must be helped (Matthew 25:35, 37, 42, 44), but also the intense spiritual desire for righteousness (Matthew 5:6). John uses it mostly in a figurative sense: in John 4:13-15, the water that Jesus gives quenches the heart's thirst forever; in John 6:35, believing in Jesus means no longer being spiritually hungry or thirsty; in John 7:37, the Holy Spirit is offered to the one who is thirsty. John 19:28 brutally recalls the physical sense: Jesus suffers thirst on the cross. Paul in 1 Corinthians 4:11 mentions the apostles who endure "thirst," and Revelation 7:16 and 21:6 promise that in eternal heaven, no one will hunger or thirst anymore.
G1372.portee: This word reveals that human needs — even the most basic — are not unworthy of God. Jesus himself suffered thirst, identifying with our frailties. But he also teaches that the true thirst that consumes the heart is not for water, but for righteousness, for meaning, for God: he alone can quench it. For the Christian, being thirsty should become a call to seek first the Kingdom and its righteousness, knowing that this thirst will be satisfied in Jesus.

sens: The physical need to drink, the drying out of the body that demands water
The ardent desire, the intense passion for something
G1373.detail:
1. Thirst is the bodily need to drink, the unpleasant state that grips one who lacks water. It is a very concrete physical sensation. Paul mentions it among his sufferings: "In toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst" (2 Corinthians 11:27), where it adds to the hunger and cold endured as a missionary.
