2. Figuratively, thirst represents the intense and deep desire for something, like a need of the heart that must be satisfied. It is the image of a thirsty heart that ardently longs for something just as the thirsty body longs for water.
G1373.origine: The word δίψος (dipsos) comes from a root that evokes the action of drying, of losing moisture. It is a later form of Greek, varying from δίψα. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, the equivalent idea is expressed by words that literally denote the state of one who lacks water. Thirst, in the Bible, is never just a simple discomfort: it is a real suffering, often associated with the desert, deprivation, and sometimes the judgment of God.
G1373.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:27, where Paul lists the deprivations he has suffered as an apostle of Christ. This mention of physical thirst is set in the context of apostolic "toils" and "labors": it is a testimony of authenticity about the reality of the sufferings endured for the Gospel. The context shows that Paul speaks of concrete bodily deprivations, not spiritual desires.
G1373.portee: For the believer, this passage reminds us that following Christ may require the acceptance of real and sometimes difficult deprivations. The thirst mentioned by Paul is not a vague metaphor, but the concrete experience of the servant of God who expends himself body and soul. It is an invitation to recognize the cost of Christian witness and not to fear suffering for the Gospel.

sens: Having two thoughts, two contradictory wills
Oscillating between two positions, unable to decide
Lacking moral constancy and stability
Divided between God and the world
G1374.detail: 1. The word depicts someone who harbors two opposing wills, like two souls battling within: in James 1:8, this man is "unstable in all his ways" and constantly changes his mind and direction, unable to hold a course. 2. It is chronic indecision: the double-minded person does not know where he is going, hesitates, doubts, and wavers between two choices without ever truly committing. 3. This weakness renders him morally and spiritually unstable: he cannot be relied upon, his promises mean nothing, and his convictions do not hold. 4. In James 4:8, the double-minded person is one who wants to please God and please the world at the same time, who claims to follow Jesus but keeps one hand clinging to earthly desires — a divided allegiance that paralyzes him.
G1374.origine: The Greek word δίψυχος (dipsuchos) is formed from δίς (dis, "two") and ψυχή (psuchè, "soul, life, will"). It literally depicts someone who has two souls or two spirits pulling in opposite directions. It is a term primarily forged in early Christian literature to describe a spiritual weakness unknown to classical Greek authors: the Bible does not borrow this word from philosophy; it invents it to name a malady diagnosed by the Holy Spirit.
G1374.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the letter of James (1:8 and 4:8). James uses it to characterize the believer who doubts: the one who prays without confidence (1:8) and the one who wants to serve two masters at the same time (4:8). The context is always spiritual and moral — it is an exhortation not to remain divided, but to turn fully toward God. The word calls the reader to examine his own heart: am I truly committed, or am I double-minded?
G1374.portee: This word invites every Christian to spiritual honesty: are we truly decided for Christ, or do we carry with us divided loyalties that weaken us? The Bible rejects half-measures and lukewarmness. Recognizing one's double-mindedness is the first step toward the conversion of the heart and the inner unity that only God can provide.

sens: The act of pursuing someone, chasing them
The suffering and trials inflicted because of faith in Christ
Organized hostility against believers and the Church
G1375.detail:
1. Persecution primarily refers to the concrete action of pursuing someone to make them suffer or force them to flee. In Acts 8:1, there is "a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem," where believers are scattered. The word evokes hunting, the pursuit carried out with hostile intent.

2. Next, the word applies to the sufferings and tribulations that disciples receive for their faith. In Matthew 13:21 and Mark 4:17, Jesus says that when "tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word," the disciples without deep roots find an occasion for stumbling. It is less about physical violence than the trials of Christian testimony.

3. More broadly, persecution describes systematic hostility against believers. In Acts 13:50, the Jews "stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas." In Romans 8:35, Paul lists persecution among the evils that could separate the believer from the love of Christ. The word encompasses both violent attacks and organized opposition from the adversaries of the Gospel.
G1375.origine: Persecution comes from the Greek διώκω (diōkō), "to pursue" or "to chase." It is a very concrete image: that of hunting, of the pursuer chasing his prey. In biblical Hebrew, the word רָדַף (radaph) carries the same idea of pursuit with intent to harm. The Greek has retained this direct image of pursuit, and the noun persecution is naturally derived from it: it is the action of pursuing to do harm.
G1375.emploi: Persecution appears 9 times in the New Testament, always to describe the opposition and suffering of believers. In the Gospels (Matthew, Mark), Jesus warns his disciples that persecution because of the word will test their faith. In Acts, it becomes a historical reality: Saul (Paul) persecutes the church (8:1), then himself suffers persecution (13:50). Paul also speaks of it as an inevitable trial for the disciple (Romans 8:35, 2 Timothy 3:11). The word remains concrete and historical, tied to specific events: the death of Stephen, the flight of believers, the opposition of Jewish or pagan authorities. It is a real suffering, not abstract.
G1375.portee: For the Christian reader, the word persecution reminds us that opposition to the message of the Gospel is not an accident, but a biblical expectation — Jesus foretold it to his disciples. This can strengthen faith in times of trial: the believer is not alone; generations of witnesses have walked the same path. On the other hand, Paul affirms that nothing, not even persecution, can separate us from the love of Christ. It is a word of courage and confidence in the very heart of adversity.

sens: One who pursues, tracks someone with the intention of harming them
One who oppresses, torments a person or group because of their beliefs or faith
One who relentlessly hunts to do harm
G1376.detail: 1. The word literally designates one who pursues someone, who chases them firmly to catch up and do them harm. It is the image of an organized hunt, a deliberate pursuit. 2. In the biblical context, it particularly applies to one who oppresses others because of their religious beliefs, faith, or group affiliation. Paul uses this term to describe his own past: "I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, a violent man" (1 Timothy 1:13), acknowledging that he actively pursued and harassed Christians before his conversion. 3. The word can also more broadly evoke one who torments or mistreats someone repeatedly and systematically, not by an isolated act, but by a persistent attitude of hostility.
G1376.origine: The word comes from the verb "diōkō" (διώκω), which fundamentally means "to pursue, to chase." This verb is itself linked to the image of hunting: one pursues an animal or an adversary. The suffix "-tēs" (-της) forms an agent noun, "one who performs the action." In Hebrew, the concept of persecution is often rendered by verbs meaning "to pursue" or "to chase," always evoking this image of relentless tracking. The persecutor is therefore "one who pursues" in a hostile manner.
G1376.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 1:13. Paul uses it to speak of himself before his encounter with Jesus on the road to Damascus: he acknowledges having been an active persecutor of Christians, pursuing them violently. This autobiographical context is fundamental: Paul does not use this word abstractly, but to confess his own past of religious violence. The term characterizes a deliberate and systematic action, not a mere opposition or occasional conflict. Through this confession, Paul shows that his conversion transformed a fierce enemy of the disciples into an apostle of Christ, hence his mention of the divine mercy that allowed him to act despite his ignorance and unbelief.
G1376.portee: For today's Christian, this word reminds us that even the worst enemies of the Church can become its zealous servants by the grace of God. Paul's confession as a former persecutor gives powerful hope: no past act is too grave for God to forgive and transform. It also invites compassion towards those who oppose Christ, as they may not know what they are doing, just like Paul. The word also warns us about the responsibility of those who persecute: it is a serious and deliberate action, not a mere difference of opinion.

sens: To put to flight, to chase
To pursue someone with hostility
To persecute, mistreat because of faith
To seek, pursue a goal or quality with zeal
To run, to hasten towards a goal
G1377.detail:
1. The most basic meaning is to chase, to put someone to flight: it is the image of someone being forced to flee (Matthew 23:34).
2. The word also means to pursue someone to reach them: it is the action of running after, either without hostile intent ("do not run after," Luke 17:23), or with a threatening intention (Acts 26:11).
3. But the main meaning in the New Testament is to persecute: to do harm to someone, to molest or imprison them because they believe in Jesus. Paul says he "persecuted this doctrine to death" (Acts 22:4), and Jesus is persecuted because of his message (John 5:16).
4. The word can also mean to seek or pursue a goal with zeal: to seek justice (Romans 9:31), love (1 Corinthians 14:1), or peace (Hebrews 12:14).
5. Finally, it expresses the idea of running or hastening: "I run to try to grasp it" (Philippians 3:12), the image being that of an athlete rushing towards the finish line.
G1377.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that expresses the idea of rapid movement, of hunting. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word רָדַף (radaf), which literally means to pursue, to chase. The family of the word includes forms that designate one who flees or one who pursues, and it always evokes a race, a quest, an action in motion.
G1377.emploi: The word appears 44 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul and in the Gospels. The meaning of to persecute largely dominates: it describes the violent opposition that Jesus' disciples suffered — Paul himself "persecuted to death" the Church (Acts 22:4, Galatians 1:13), and Jesus reminds believers: "If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you" (John 15:20). Matthew and Luke speak of it as a blessing: "Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake" (Matthew 5:10-12). The word also applies to the ardent pursuit of virtues: one "pursues" justice, peace, love (Romans 9:30-31, 1 Corinthians 14:1, Hebrews 12:14). Finally, in a few passages, it retains the neutral meaning of running after or hastening towards a goal (Luke 17:23, Philippians 3:12).
G1377.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that faith in Jesus comes at a cost: disciples are called to accept persecution, not with shame, but as part of their commitment to him. At the same time, it shows that this same zeal — this same energy, this same "running" — must be applied to the pursuit of Christian virtues: justice, peace, love. Persecution is not an end in itself; it is the call to pursue Christ himself with the same intensity that the early Church endured attacks.

sens: Official decree issued by a political authority (emperor, king)
Rule or ordinance established by an assembly or institution
Prescription of the Jewish Law
Collective decision of a group of leaders
G1378.detail:
1. An edict is primarily an official proclamation made by a sovereign authority, particularly a Roman emperor. Luke 2:1 provides an example with the edict of Caesar Augustus ordering the census of all the land: it is a commanding order that all must obey.
2. An edict can also be a rule established by an assembly of leaders, as when the apostles and elders of Jerusalem make a decision and the disciples are invited to observe it (Acts 16:4). It is less the voice of a single sovereign than the will of a group holding authority.
3. The Jewish Law itself is described as a set of ordinances or edicts that God has established (Ephesians 2:15, Colossians 2:14). These prescriptions were binding and weighed on those who did not respect them.
4. In the background, an edict always implies a will that imposes itself: someone must obey what has been decreed, under penalty of sanction.
G1378.origine: The word comes from the ancient Greek δοκέω (dokéô), which means "to seem" or "to appear." An edict is thus what has been "judged good" or "judged useful" by the one who commands, and then promulgated. It represents the thought, opinion, or judgment of an authority that has become law. In Hebrew, it corresponds mainly to דָּת (dât, "law") and to טְעֵם (taaʿam, "decision"), particularly in the later writings of the Old Testament where Persian kings issue decrees.
G1378.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament. It first refers to the edicts of Roman emperors (Luke 2:1 for the census; Acts 17:7 where it is contrasted with the laws of Caesar). Then, it qualifies the decisions made by the apostles and elders of the Church (Acts 16:4), showing that the early Church saw itself as invested with an authority that produces binding rules. Finally, Paul uses it twice to speak of the ordinances of the Mosaic Law (Ephesians 2:15 and Colossians 2:14): these legal prescriptions had the character of mandatory edicts, but Christ abolished their force by offering Himself on the cross.
G1378.portee: The word reminds us that all authority — whether Roman, apostolic, or divine — expresses itself through ordinances intended to govern the lives of those who recognize it. The mention of Caesar's edicts shows how the Empire imposes its will; the mention of apostolic decisions shows how the early Church builds its unity through common rules. Above all, the use of the word for the Law reveals a decisive truth: the Mosaic ordinances were not suggestions, but commandments weighing on the conscience, until Christ fulfilled them and freed us through His death and resurrection.

sens: Issue a decree, an official ordinance
Subject someone to a rule, an obligation
Subject to ritual or legal practices
G1379.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to issuing a decree or ordinance with authority: it is the action of a power that sets a mandatory rule for all (like when a king decrees a law). 2. But in the Epistle to the Colossians, it carries a more personal idea of subjecting someone to a rule, imposing an obligation on them. Paul asks: why are you being imposed upon with precepts as if you still needed to be bound to the practices of the world? 3. In a biblical context, this verb mainly applies to imposing ritual practices or legal observances: it is to subject to external rules, often deemed excessive or unnecessary once one has received freedom in Christ.
G1379.origine: The word comes from "dogma" (δόγμα), which means a decision, an ordinance, a decree established by authority. It is an administrative and official term. The verb "dogmatizō" adds the idea of acting according to this decree, being its author, or applying it. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word "kâtab" (to write an ordinance) and "dâth" (law, ordinance). The image is that of public power imposing its will through decree.
G1379.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Colossians 2:20. Paul uses it to criticize those who would impose legalistic rules on Christians, as if the death and resurrection with Christ had not been enough to free them. He opposes the spiritual freedom gained in Christ. The tone is polemical: Paul questions the authority of these "worldly" ordinances in light of the lordship of Christ.
G1379.portee: This word reminds the Christian that he should not submit to human impositions that contradict the freedom acquired in Christ. It encourages discernment between the true commandments of God and the traditions or rules that claim to bind us. It is an invitation to live not by fear or guilt imposed from the outside, but by love and free obedience to Jesus.

sens: Have an opinion, a conviction about something
Seem, appear in a certain way
Think, judge that something is true or good
Be reputed, enjoy a certain consideration
Consider good, find suitable
G1380.detail:
1. To have an opinion, a conviction: it is to form a personal judgment about something. In 1 Corinthians 8:2, the one who "thinks he knows" something shows that he has a subjective conviction, not true knowledge. It is to believe firmly based on one's own reasoning.
2. To seem, to appear: it is the impression that something produces on the observer. When the disciples saw Jesus walking on the water, they "thought they saw a spirit" (Luke 24:37) — it seemed to them to be a spirit. In Mark 10:42, those who are "looked upon" as leaders seem to be so in the eyes of others.
3. To think, to judge: it is to form a judgment about what is true, good, or suitable. In Matthew 3:9, John the Baptist warns the Pharisees: do not "pretend" (do not believe, do not think) that being children of Abraham is enough.
4. To be reputed, to have a good reputation: it is to enjoy esteem, consideration in the eyes of others. In Galatians 2:6, Paul speaks of "those who are esteemed highly" — those who are considered important — to signify that their reputation does not change the truth.
5. To consider good, to find suitable: it is to judge that an action is appropriate or pleasant. In Acts 15:25, the apostles "thought it good" to choose delegates, meaning they deemed it good and useful.
G1380.origine: The word comes from a root expressing opinion and personal impression. It is related to "doxa" (opinion, glory) and to verbs meaning to receive or accept. In Hebrew, it often translates verbs like "to be good" or "to be voluntary." The Greek word δοκέω always emphasizes the point of view of the subject who judges: what I believe, what seems to me, what I estimate.
G1380.emploi: The verb δοκέω is used 63 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Pauline epistles. It primarily expresses a personal opinion ("think he knows," "think he sees") or a judgment on the value or suitability of something ("consider," "judge"). The context determines the nuance: when it concerns what one thinks of a person, it can mean "to be reputed" or "to enjoy consideration." The Bible uses it to show how men judge — often superficially or erroneously — in contrast to the true knowledge that God provides.
G1380.portee: This word reminds the reader that our opinions and impressions are not certainties. We "believe" many things that seem obvious to us, while they may be false. True Christian faith transcends these simple subjective beliefs: it rests on the revelation of God, not on what we "think." This word invites us to distinguish between human opinion and divine knowledge.

sens: To submit something to a test to verify its quality, strength, or value
To put someone or oneself to the test to verify sincerity, faith, or fidelity
To discern, distinguish, or recognize something by careful examination
To judge worthy, approve, or consider acceptable after examination
G1381.detail:
1. The primary meaning, derived from the metallurgical image, signifies submitting something to a test to verify its quality or true nature. Pure gold "tested by fire" (1 Peter 1:7) emerges strengthened from the test; spirits are also tested, meaning their divine origin is examined (1 John 4:1) or the conformity of a work to God's judgment is verified (1 Corinthians 3:13).
2. The word also applies to putting a person to the test: testing deacons before admitting them (1 Timothy 3:10), examining oneself to verify the sincerity of one's faith (2 Corinthians 13:5), or testing the genuine charity of a community (2 Corinthians 8:8).
3. "To test" can also mean "to discern" or "to recognize" through careful examination: discerning what time demands (Luke 12:56), or identifying what is excellent and worthy of approval (Philippians 1:10).
4. As a result of this examination, the word means "to approve" or "to judge good": after testing, one recognizes a person as trustworthy, or one deems a practice suitable (Romans 14:22).
G1381.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to approve" or "to judge acceptable," hence the image of a touchstone that allows testing of genuine gold or silver. In Hebrew, the Bible primarily uses the verb "bahan" (בָּחַן), which carries the same idea of testing: God "tests" hearts and reins, as one tests metal in fire. The central notion is that of a trial that reveals the true nature of a thing or a person.
G1381.emploi: This verb appears about twenty times, mainly in the Pauline epistles and in 1 Peter and 1 John. The Apostle Paul uses it to exhort Christians to examine themselves and test their faith (2 Corinthians 13:5, Galatians 6:4), or to invite them to discern the will of God (Romans 12:2, Ephesians 5:10). The word also describes how God tests hearts (1 Thessalonians 2:4) or how fire will judge works on the final day (1 Corinthians 3:13). In 1 Peter 1:7, gold tested by fire symbolizes faith subjected to tribulation. Everywhere, "to test" implies a judgment that separates the true from the false, the worthy from the rejected.
G1381.portee: This word reminds Christians that their faith is not static, but is tested to be strengthened. Examining one's own sincerity, discerning the will of God, testing spirits to recognize those who come from God — this is the call to a life of discernment and vigilance. The image of metal in fire invites one to see tribulation not as mere suffering, but as a process that purifies and reveals the true nature of what one believes and does.

sens: The action of testing, verifying, or examining
The result of this test: approval, proof
What manifests the quality or value of a person or thing
G1382.detail:
1. The test is the action of submitting something or someone to a trial to see its true nature. It is to test, verify, examine: Paul writes to the Corinthians that he tests them to know if they are obedient (2 Corinthians 2:9), and Timothy was tested in serving the Gospel with Paul to show his faithfulness (Philippians 2:22).
2. The test is also the result, the approval: when a person successfully passes the test, they obtain proof of their value. Perseverance produces victory, a test overcome that strengthens hope (Romans 5:4). Likewise, an authentic proof that Christ speaks through Paul is His power manifested among the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 13:3).
3. The test sometimes designates what serves as visible proof, a certificate of value: the generosity of the Corinthians is a concrete proof that God is working in them and that the Gospel is true (2 Corinthians 9:13).
G1382.origine: The word comes from the Greek δόκιμος (dokimos), which means "tested," "approved." It is a key word in the ancient world: metals, soldiers, orators had to be tested to be certified. The root evokes the idea of putting to the test to separate the true from the false, the solid from the fragile. In Hebrew, this word often translates the idea of "test" (בחן bachan), which also means to test or examine.
G1382.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul. It first denotes the action of testing (2 Corinthians 2:9: to test to verify obedience; Philippians 2:22: to be tested in serving). It also denotes the positive result of this test, the approval that follows: perseverance produces a "victory" that strengthens faith (Romans 5:4), or the proof of Christ's power (2 Corinthians 13:3). The test sometimes becomes the visible sign, the concrete demonstration: the generosity of the Corinthians is a living proof of their faith (2 Corinthians 9:13). The word evolves between the process and the fruit: to test, then to be approved.
G1382.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that faith is not abstract: it is tested, it is proven through actions and perseverance. The difficulties we go through are not in vain; they produce an approval, an inner certainty that our faith is real. The test is the path that leads to assurance. This also invites us not to flee from tests: what puts us to the test purifies us and brings us closer to God.

sens: The act of being tested
What tests faith and solidifies it
The result or product of this test: the recognized quality after the trial
G1383.detail:
1. The test is the moment when faith is put to the test, that is, tested by difficulties. Just as gold is tested by putting it in fire to verify its purity (1 Peter 1:7), God allows difficulties to test our faith to see if it is genuine.
2. It is also what tests us: the trials themselves, the difficult situations we go through. James says that the test of your faith "produces patience" (James 1:3) — it is through difficulties that we become patient.
3. The word can also designate the recognized result: the approved value that appears when one has endured the test. Gold tested by fire becomes even more precious; faith tested by difficulties gains in strength and deserves praise.
G1383.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to test," "to prove." It is very close to the word "docimé" which means "approved after testing." The basic image is that of the tester who puts metal in fire to judge its purity — a well-known practice in antiquity. This vocabulary of testing and approval appears several times in Paul to speak of faith and Christian character.
G1383.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in letters addressed to communities in difficulty. James uses it to urge his readers to see in their trials a means that God uses to develop their patience (James 1:3). Peter takes up the same word to encourage persecuted Christians to understand that their sufferings purify their faith as fire purifies gold, and that this purified faith will ultimately receive praise when Christ appears (1 Peter 1:7). In both cases, the test is not a punishment, but a process of maturation.
G1383.portee: This word invites the believer to change perspective in the face of difficulties. Instead of seeing trials as a gratuitous evil or a mark of God's displeasure, the Bible presents them as a test that produces fruit: patience, strength of character, a tested and therefore real faith. For those who suffer, understanding that their trial has spiritual value — that it purifies them as fire purifies gold — can be a source of courage and confidence in God.

sens: Who has successfully undergone a trial and has been recognized as authentic or conforming
Who has received approval or endorsement from someone
Who has proven trustworthy through actions and behavior
G1384.detail:
1. The word δόκιμος first evokes the image of precious metals: an alloy of silver or gold that is passed through fire to verify its purity and quality. Once the trial is passed, the metal is 'approved,' meaning judged authentic and of good quality. In 2 Timothy 2:15, Paul urges Timothy to present himself before God 'as a proven man,' meaning someone who has survived the trial and emerged purified and reliable.
2. The word also designates one who enjoys the approval of a recognized authority. In Romans 14:18, the one who serves Christ faithfully is 'approved' by men — he has gained their esteem because he has proven trustworthy. In 2 Corinthians 10:18, Paul teaches that the one whom the Lord approves is truly approved, much more than the one who commends himself.
3. More broadly, the word characterizes the person or action that has proven itself and can be counted as reliable. In 1 Corinthians 11:19, Paul says that divisions reveal 'those who are approved' among you — those whose faith has solidified through trial and who testify to it.
G1384.origine: The word δόκιμος derives from δοκιμή ('trial, test') and the verb δοκιμάζω ('to prove, test'). Its basic image is metallurgical: it is often found in Greek literature to describe a metal that has passed the test of fire. In the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament), it translates the Hebrew זָקַק in the passive ('to be refined, purified'), the process by which gold or silver is purified from dross in the fire. This biblical image of the test by fire has enriched to spiritually designate one who has remained faithful in trial.
G1384.emploi: δόκιμος appears 7 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul's epistles. Paul uses it to describe one who has successfully passed the trial: Apelles is 'approved in Christ' (Romans 16:10), and the faithful servant of Christ becomes 'approved' in the eyes of God and men (Romans 14:18). The word also characterizes spiritual authenticity: in 1 Corinthians 11:19, the 'approved' believers are those whose faith has proven solid amid divisions. Paul plays on the antithesis between what the Lord approves and what man judges (2 Corinthians 10:18, 13:7). In 2 Timothy 2:15, Timothy is called to become a 'proven' worker, based on a right understanding of the Word. The word always retains this dual dimension: the trial already endured and the approval gained.
G1384.portee: This word reminds the believer that their faith and faithfulness are not a matter of reputation or image, but of real trial and divine approval. To be 'approved' means having been tested and proven worthy — it is a promise for those who persevere. It invites the reader to seek not the approval of men, but that of God, which alone has true value. It is also a call to sincerity: unlike counterfeit money, the believer whose faith is solid has nothing to fear from examination.

sens: Large piece of wood that supports a structure
Image of hypocrisy: a serious flaw that one does not see in oneself
G1385.detail:
1. The word literally refers to a large beam, a thick squared piece of wood used in framing to support the floors or roof of a house. It is a concrete and striking image: much larger and bulkier than a speck of dust.
2. Jesus uses this image in his teaching on judgment: it is absurd and hypocritical to want to remove a tiny speck from your brother's eye when you have a large beam in your own eye (Matthew 7:3-5, Luke 6:41-42). The beam represents a serious flaw, a major fault in the one who judges, while the speck is a minor flaw in the one being judged. Jesus teaches that one must first correct oneself before pretending to correct others.
G1385.origine: The Greek word dokos comes from the root dekhomai (to receive), because a beam receives and supports the weight of the structure. In Hebrew, one would say qora for a framing beam. The word is used only in the literal sense in the Gospels, but it becomes immediately figurative through Jesus' own teaching.
G1385.emploi: The word beam appears only in two parallel passages in the New Testament: the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew (7:3-5) and the similar discourse in Luke (6:41-42). These two accounts report exactly the same teaching of Jesus, with the same images of the beam and the speck. Nowhere else is the word used to designate a true building beam: its use is entirely figurative and pedagogical, to criticize the hypocrisy of judgment.
G1385.portee: This image of the beam and the speck teaches the believer an essential clarity: before judging or correcting others, one must honestly examine their own flaws, often much more serious than they believe. It is a call to humility and sincerity towards oneself, a condition for any just criticism of a brother.

sens: One who uses cunning, lies, or bad faith to deceive others
One whose appearance or promises cannot be trusted
One who acts with hidden malice and intention
G1386.detail:
1. The word describes someone who deliberately uses cunning and lies to deceive others. This is not a simple mistake or clumsiness, but intentional and conscious deception. In 2 Corinthians 11:13, Paul calls the false apostles who pretend to serve Christ while sowing error as such.
2. A 'deceiver' is also one whose appearance or words do not reflect reality: one cannot trust him, as he hides his true intentions behind a mask. The false apostles of Paul are a perfect example: they 'disguise themselves as apostles of Christ,' but their hearts seek to mislead the disciples.
3. The deceiver acts with hidden malice; he is not simply erroneous but malicious: he deliberately seeks to harm by exploiting the trust of others.
G1386.origine: The word comes from the root δόλος (dolos), which means 'cunning,' 'deception,' 'trickery.' This root also appears in other Greek words in the New Testament such as δολεύω (to act with cunning). It is a rich word, evoking the image of a trap set or an ambush: the deceiver is one who secretly prepares his deception.
G1386.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:13. Paul uses it to describe the false apostles who infiltrated the churches of Corinth. These men presented themselves as servants of Christ and claimed to bring true teaching, but Paul reveals their true nature: they are 'deceivers,' meaning they intentionally act to deceive and mislead naive believers. It is a serious term in Paul's mouth, who fights to preserve the integrity of his Gospel.
G1386.portee: This word invites the Christian to vigilance: do not naively believe everything that bears the name of Christ or hides behind a beautiful appearance. It also calls us to honesty towards ourselves and others, rejecting all cunning or malicious intention in our own lives. It is a term that sheds light on the real spiritual battle that Paul describes: the constant temptation of imposture within the Church itself.

sens: Lead someone astray by word or action
Use cunning or lies to make someone believe the false
Abuse the trust of others through duplicity
G1387.detail:
1. To deceive is to make someone believe the false, to lead someone astray by saying or doing what is not true. The image is that of someone who intentionally diverts the truth to take advantage of another. In Romans 3:13, Paul quotes a psalm to show that wicked men "use their tongues to deceive": their flattering and lying words help mislead those who listen to them.
2. Deceiving involves malicious intent, calculated cunning. It is not a simple unintentional mistake, but a deliberate act of deception. It is to use lies or falsehoods to gain an advantage over someone else.
3. This verb also describes the abuse of trust: the one who deceives takes advantage of the good faith of the one who believes him, profiting from their naivety or trust to dupe them.
G1387.origine: The Greek word δολιόω comes from δόλιος (dolios), which means "full of cunning" or "deceitful." The root evokes the image of lying and duplicity. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses similar verbs like נָכַל (nakhal, "to deceive by cunning") and חָלַק (chalaq in the active voice, "to act with falsehood"). This Greek word regularly translates these Hebrew roots in the Greek version of the Old Testament, showing that the notion of intentional lying runs through both testaments.
G1387.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 3:13. Paul borrows it from the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament, to describe the character of sinful men. By quoting Psalm 5, he shows that those who reject God are characterized by deceit: their throat is an open grave (they spread death), their tongue deceives (they use lies), and under their lips is the poison of asps (they hide the poison of wickedness). It is a striking portrait of human depravity when given over to evil.
G1387.portee: This word reminds Christians that lying and deceit are among the symptoms of a heart separated from God. Jesus himself said that lies come from the devil, the "father of lies" (John 8:44). Recognizing that we are all capable of deception urges us to be vigilant against hypocrisy, to seek authenticity in our words and actions, and to praise the absolute truth that Jesus embodies. It is a call to sincerity and integrity in all circumstances.

sens: Trap or bait set to catch someone
Hidden scheme to deceive or manipulate
Dishonesty, malice in intentions or words
G1388.detail:
1. The word first evokes an action of tenderness or a physical trap: in Matthew 26:4 and Mark 14:1, the chief priests seek to arrest Jesus "by cunning," meaning by taking him through a roundabout and hidden means, rather than openly.
2. More broadly, it refers to any scheme intended to deceive: in Acts 13:10, Paul denounces someone as "full of all kinds of cunning and deceit," describing a habit of manipulation and deception. It is the art of concealing one's true intentions to achieve one's goal.
3. In a moral sense, it is the absence of sincerity and honesty of heart. Jesus praises Nathanael by saying: "there is no deceit in him" (John 1:47), which means that Nathanael is transparent, without hidden calculation. It is the opposite of a right conscience.
G1388.origine: The Greek word δόλος comes from an ancient Indo-European root that evokes the idea of deceiving or binding. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew *mirmah*, which literally means "deceit" or "falsehood." It is a word that always describes an action or disposition of the heart oriented towards lying and manipulating others.
G1388.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, mostly in the epistles. It is always pejorative: it describes either a hidden action to harm (the arrest of Jesus by cunning in Matthew 26:4), or a corrupted disposition of the heart. In Paul, in Romans 1:29 and Acts 13:10, it appears in a list of serious vices. Peter uses it to urge believers to put away all cunning (1 Peter 2:1) and reminds that Jesus "committed no sin, and there was no deceit in his mouth" (1 Peter 2:22). The context shows that it is a serious evil, contrary to justice and holiness.
G1388.portee: For the Christian, this word is a call to radical honesty of heart. Jesus praises Nathanael for the absence of cunning in him; he is a model of total sincerity. Peter urges to reject "all cunning" (1 Peter 2:1), which means not to seek to deceive through hidden means, but to act in the light and truth. It is a reminder that the disciple of Christ must be transparent like Jesus himself.

sens: Corrupt, adulterate a substance (like wine)
Distort, falsify a message or word
G1389.detail:
1. The word first evokes the action of corrupting or adulterating a substance — for example, mixing wine with water or other products to denature it and make it unfit. This is the primary, concrete sense: one "alters" what was pure.
2. By extension, it means to distort or falsify a word, a teaching, a truth. In 2 Corinthians 4:2, Paul says he does not "alter" the word of God: he does not dilute it with lies or compromises, he does not falsify it to please men or serve hidden interests. It is to keep the received truth intact.
G1389.origine: The word comes from δόλος (dolos, cunning, deceit). The verb δολόω literally means "to act with cunning" or "to corrupt by deceit." The image is that of the deceiver who mixes a pure substance with another so that it goes unnoticed. In the Greek Old Testament, it is applied to acts of deception or falsehood.
G1389.emploi: The word appears only once in 2 Corinthians 4:2. Paul uses it in his apostolic defense: he asserts that, unlike false apostles or preachers who distort the Gospel for mercenary or selfish reasons, he and his companions refuse to "corrupt" or "falsify" the word of God. It is an act of fidelity to the message received from the Lord.
G1389.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the integrity of Christian preaching and teaching. To alter the word of God is to mix it with lies or human interests. Refusing to alter it means transmitting it as it was received, in all its purity and truth, without bending it to the compromises of the world. It is an exhortation to faithfulness and authenticity in the ministry of the Word.

sens: Present, object offered freely
Act of giving, generosity
Ability or favor granted by God
G1390.detail: 1. The gift is primarily a concrete object offered to someone without compensation, a present. In Matthew 7:11 and Luke 11:13, Jesus speaks of the "good things" that fathers give to their children: material gifts, everyday presents. 2. The word also refers to the act of giving itself, generosity in action. In Ephesians 4:8, the risen Christ "gave gifts to men," meaning he distributed abilities and graces to the entire Church. 3. By extension, the gift becomes a spiritual favor, an ability or privilege received from God. In Philippians 4:17, Paul seeks "the fruit that abounds to your account" rather than the material gifts themselves: he aims for the blessing that God brings through the gifts, not the presents for what they are.
G1390.origine: The word δόμα comes from the Greek verb δίδωμι (didômi), "to give." It translates the Hebrew מַתָּנָה (mattana), which also means "gift" or "present." The root evokes the simple and primitive idea of offering, of placing into someone else's hands. In the New Testament, it belongs to a rich family: δόσις (dosís, "act of giving"), δῶρον (dôron, "gift" or "offering"), δωρεά (dôrea, "grace given"), and δώρημα (dôrêma, "present"), each nuance the idea of gift from a slightly different angle.
G1390.emploi: The word δόμα appears four times in the New Testament, all cited here. In Matthew and Luke, it refers to the simple presents that fathers give to their children to illustrate how generous God is to those who ask him. In Ephesians 4:8, quoted from Psalm 68, the gift becomes an eschatological reality: the exalted Christ distributes spiritual gifts to his Church, abilities and ministries for the common edification. In Philippians 4:17, Paul puts material gifts into perspective: what matters is the spiritual fruit that results, the blessing that multiplies. The word thus embodies the transition from concrete and everyday gifts to spiritual and divine gifts.
G1390.portee: The gift reveals the generous nature of God and Christ. Jesus teaches that God gives much more willingly and better than our earthly fathers do: this is an assurance for prayer and trust. In Ephesians, understanding that Christ distributes gifts invites every believer to recognize in themselves an ability received, a ministry to exercise for the Church. In Philippians, Paul warns us: the gift is never an end in itself, but the means of blessing. This frees us from mercantilism and anchors Christian generosity in a perspective of spiritual fruit.

sens: The honor and reputation enjoyed by a person among others
The praise, consideration, and respect given to someone
The brilliance, splendor, luminosity emanating from a presence or being
The visible manifestation of God's presence, his divine radiance
The blessed and glorious condition that believers will receive at Christ's return
The merit or accomplishment worthy of praise
G1391.detail:
1. The honor a person receives from others: it is their reputation, the respect in which they are held. John 5:44 shows Jesus reproaching his listeners for seeking "the glory that comes from men" instead of that which comes from God.
2. The praise, honor, and respect that is intentionally given to someone. Giving glory to God means publicly acknowledging him as worthy of all honor (Romans 4:20: Abraham "glorified God").
3. The luminous brilliance, the visible splendor: the radiant light of a remarkable presence. At Cana, Jesus "manifested his glory" by performing a miracle (John 2:11), showing through visible acts who he truly is.
4. The luminous and radiant presence of God himself, his divine brilliance that man cannot sustain without fear. In 2 Corinthians 4:6, Paul speaks of "the glory of God" shining from the face of Christ, the living image of who God is.
5. The glorious joy, the eternal happiness that God will grant to believers when Christ returns (1 Peter 4:13: sharing "in the sufferings of Christ" leads to sharing in his glory to come).
6. What is worthy of praise or pride, the magnificent accomplishment of a work. Luke 2:14 proclaims "Glory to God in the highest," celebrating the infinite worth of his salvation plan.
G1391.origine: The Greek word δόξα comes from the verb δοκέω ("to seem, appear, be of the opinion"), initially expressing "what seems good," "the opinion one has of someone." Gradually, the meaning enriches to denote not only the impression received but the honor and splendor that emanates from it. In the Greek Bible (Septuagint), this word regularly translates the Hebrew כָּבוֹד (kabod), which literally means "weight, heaviness," evoking major importance and prestige. This Hebrew root also suggests "richness" and "abundance": glory is what weighs heavily, what truly matters, and what impresses by its brilliance. For God, "glory" denotes his radiant presence and honor that no creature can equal.
G1391.emploi: The word δόξα appears about 150 times in the New Testament. It is very frequent in Paul (letters to the Romans, Corinthians, Ephesians), in the Gospel of John, and in the epistles. In the Synoptics, it often signifies visible brilliance: "the glory" of the Son of Man at judgment (Matthew 24:30, Mark 13:26), or the magnificence of the kingdoms of the world that the devil shows to Jesus (Matthew 4:8). In John, the word takes on a particular theological density: the glory of Jesus is manifested in his miracles (John 2:11), it is the glory he possessed with the Father before the world began (John 17:5), and it is promised to believers (John 17:22). Paul strongly emphasizes the future glory of the elect (Romans 8:18, 21) and the duty to give glory to God in all actions (1 Corinthians 10:31). The word can be nuanced: it denotes the honor sought from men (to be avoided: John 5:44), the honor given to God (Romans 4:20), the visible manifestation of the divine (2 Corinthians 4:6), or the eternal condition of the redeemed (Romans 5:2).
G1391.portee: Understanding biblical "glory" refocuses our values. Seeking glory from men (John 5:44) is a constant temptation for believers; the Bible invites us to prefer the honor that comes from God alone. Giving glory to God is not an empty formula: it is practically recognizing his sovereignty in all that we do (1 Corinthians 10:31). The promise of a future and eternal "glory" for the elect grounds Christian hope: our present sufferings are light labors "in comparison to this glory" (Romans 8:18). Finally, contemplating in Jesus Christ the manifestation of divine glory transforms the believer (2 Corinthians 3:18), progressively revealing the beauty and majesty of who God is.

sens: To attribute honor and renown to someone, to praise and exalt them
To recognize the splendor and power of someone, to honor them through actions or words
To make manifest the glory of God, to shine forth His power and beauty
To make glorious, to adorn with splendor and honor
To become famous, to gain renown
G1392.detail:
1. To glorify is primarily to honor someone by praising and exalting them. When the disciples saw Jesus heal the paralytic, "all [...] glorified God" (Luke 5:26): they recognized His power and praised Him. It is an act of acknowledgment before the greatness of someone.

2. To glorify also means to honor someone by bringing them to the forefront, by illuminating their glory. The people who witnessed the miracles "glorified God" by saying it was His work. Jesus tells His disciples: "Glorify God in your body" (1 Corinthians 6:20), meaning show through your life that God is great and worthy of respect.

3. When the Holy Spirit "will glorify" Jesus (John 16:14), it means He will make Him known and recognized for who He truly is: the Son of God. It is to make visible and manifest the hidden glory of someone.

4. Sometimes, to glorify also means to adorn with splendor: Moses' face was glorified when it shone after his encounter with God. God "glorifies" us by transforming us into His image and giving us a share of His splendor.

5. Finally, the word can mean "to become famous, to gain renown": when people "glorify" someone, they make known their name and reputation.
G1392.origine: The word comes from δόξα (doxa = glory, opinion, renown). Its root is related to "to appear," "to have the appearance of." In Hebrew, the verb often translating this Greek word is כָּבַד (kabad = to be heavy, important, honorable), which evokes the idea of weight and importance. To glorify God is to acknowledge His weight, His importance, His greatness in the cosmos and our lives. The word can also appear with the prefix "en-" (ἐνδοξάζω) or "with-" (συνδοξάζω) to reinforce the idea.
G1392.emploi: The verb δοξάζω appears about 54 times in the New Testament, especially in John and the epistles. It primarily denotes the honor given to God: the apostles "glorify" God when they recognize His works (Acts 11:18). In John, it takes on a particular depth: Jesus asks the Father to glorify Him (John 17:1, 17:5), which means to give Him a place of eternal splendor. The disciples also "glorify" Jesus by recognizing and worshiping Him. Paul uses it to exhort believers: "Glorify God in your body" (1 Corinthians 6:20) — this is a call to live in a way that honors God's name. The word can also evoke the transformation that God works in us: we will be "glorified" at the resurrection (Romans 8:30). The usage thus varies between the act of praising and the state of being adorned with glory.
G1392.portee: To glorify God is at the heart of the Christian life: to recognize His greatness and honor Him through our words and actions. This word calls the believer to live in such a way that God is brought to light in their life. It is also a promise: God promises to glorify us, to transform us, and to give us a place of splendor in His eternal kingdom. Finally, recognizing that only God is worthy of glory frees us from idolatry and the love of human honors.

sens: Christian woman from Joppa, disciple of Christ
one who does charitable works for the poor
G1393.detail:
1. Dorcas is a believing woman who lives in Joppa during the time of the apostles (Acts 9:36). Her Aramaic name, Tabitha, means "gazelle" — a light and graceful creature. She is known in the local church as a woman filled with good works and generous in her almsgiving.
2. What makes Dorcas renowned is her skill and practical love: she sews tunics and garments for the poor widows in the community (Acts 9:39). After her death, Peter raises her from the dead, so precious was her ministry of service to the disciples.
G1393.origine: The name Dorcas is the Greek form of the Aramaic word Tabitha (תביתא). In Greek, dorkas means "gazelle" — a swift and graceful animal from the Mediterranean region. This name evokes agility and elegance. Both names refer to the same person: the Segond first gives the Aramaic name, then the Greek translation.
G1393.emploi: Dorcas appears twice in Acts (9:36 and 9:39), always in relation to the same woman and the same event. She is first presented in Joppa as a remarkable disciple known for her good works (9:36). Then, when she falls ill and dies, the widows she served with her handiwork weep around Peter and show him the garments she made for them (9:39). It is an emotional picture of the impact of a humble and generous ministry in the early Christian community. Peter raises her, thus manifesting the power of Christ.
G1393.portee: Dorcas embodies the heart of Christian service: doing concrete good for the poor and the widows, not out of obligation but out of love. Her story shows that humble works — sewing a garment — have infinite value in the eyes of God and His Church. She reminds the believer that active charity is the living expression of faith.

sens: the act of giving
that which is given, a present
G1394.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of giving itself, the action of handing something over to someone. Paul writes to the Philippians: "no church entered into partnership with me in giving and receiving" — he speaks of their act of sharing with him, their active generosity.
2. Next, the word denotes the object given, the present received. James says: "every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights" — he speaks of the gifts, the presents that God gives us, particularly the grace that comes from Him.
G1394.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb δίδωμι (to give). It properly denotes the action or the result of that action. It is a noun constructed from the root of the verb "to give," just as in French "don" comes from "donner." The Greek Bible uses it to translate the Hebrew חֹק, which means a portion, a share assigned to someone — the common idea is that of a distribution, an allocation.
G1394.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Philippians 4:15, Paul uses it to refer to the act of giving, the generous contribution of the Philippians who supported him financially. In James 1:17, it is "gift" in the sense of the received present, and the context specifically speaks of spiritual gifts — the grace and blessings that God gives us. The same word thus covers both the act (to give) and its fruit (that which is given), showing the unity between generosity and what it produces.
G1394.portee: This word reminds the reader that Christian generosity is not a vague feeling, but a concrete act — "to give." It also invites us to recognize that everything we have, all that is good in us, ultimately comes from God as a gift. Grace itself is the greatest "gift" we receive.

sens: one who gives
one who makes a gift
one who offers joyfully
G1395.detail:
1. The giver is simply one who gives, who offers something to someone else. This is the active person in the act of giving.
2. In the biblical context, the giver is one who contributes voluntarily, for example by giving money or goods for a cause. Paul speaks of one who gives without compulsion, freely (2 Corinthians 9:7).
3. The cheerful giver is particularly valued: God prefers one who gives with joy and goodwill, rather than one who gives out of obligation or under pressure. It is the heart of the giver that matters.
G1395.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb δίδωμι (to give). The suffix -της (-tēs) creates an agent noun: one who performs the action. It is a variant of another form, δοτήρ (dotēr), which also means "giver." In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses analogous roots to speak of one who gives.
G1395.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 9:7, where Paul encourages the Christians in Corinth to contribute to the support of the poor believers in Jerusalem. In this unique passage, Paul emphasizes the attitude of the giver: he must give voluntarily, without feeling of compulsion or sadness, for God loves a cheerful giver. It is a fundamental lesson on Christian generosity.
G1395.portee: This word reminds us that God sees the attitude of the giver, not just the amount of the gift. It invites us to examine our hearts when we give: do we give out of duty, social pressure, or sincere joy? True generosity arises from a joyful and willing heart, never from compulsion. It is a word that frees the Christian and turns him toward the joy of sharing.

sens: To reduce someone to slavery, to place under a yoke
To submit one's body or desires to strict discipline
G1396.detail:
1. The basic meaning is to reduce someone to slavery or to completely dominate them as one dominates a slave: to take away their freedom and force them to obey. It is the image of a person who loses their autonomy and becomes entirely submissive to another.
2. In a figurative and spiritual sense, it is to submit one's body, impulses, or appetites to a rigid discipline to achieve a goal: this is what Paul does in 1 Corinthians 9:27 when he says, "I discipline my body and keep it under control," meaning he tames it, masters it through effort, as one masters a rebellious slave.
G1396.origine: The Greek word δουλαγωγέω comes from two elements: δοῦλος (doûlos, "slave") and ἄγω (agô, "to lead, to bring"). The image is of someone who leads, who guides—but as a master leads a slave, with absolute authority. It literally means "to lead into slavery" or "to conduct as one conducts a slave." The composition suggests a voluntary act of enslavement: one takes something free and makes it captive.
G1396.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 9:27, in a very strong personal and spiritual context. Paul speaks of how he treats his own body: he puts it "under the yoke," he disciplines it. It is a verb that expresses a deliberate action, a constant effort to master carnal desires and maintain spiritual discipline. Paul uses this strong image to show that he does not let his body or passions command—he commands them, as one commands a slave.
G1396.portee: This word invites the Christian to meditate on the necessity of disciplining their body and appetites to live a life faithful to the Gospel. Paul shows us that Christian freedom is not the absence of all constraint, but rather the ability to master what would enslave us—sin, selfishness, carnal desires. It is a courageous call to spiritual vigilance: one who wants to proclaim the Gospel must first live it, by submitting their body to the authority of the Spirit.

sens: State of one who is a slave, submitted to a master
Condition of captivity or oppression
State of fear that paralyzes and enslaves
Subjection to a law or a binding principle
G1397.detail:
1. Servitude is primarily the state of a person reduced to slavery, forced to obey without freedom. This is the concrete meaning of the word in the ancient biblical context.
2. More broadly, it is any form of captivity or oppression that takes away freedom — the slavery of sin or death, for example. Hebrews 2:15 speaks of those "held in servitude" by the fear of death.
3. Servitude also refers to the state of mind of one who lives in fear and emotional enslavement. Romans 8:15 contrasts the "spirit of servitude" (which keeps one in fear) with the Spirit of adoption that cries, "Abba! Father!".
4. It can refer to subjection to a law or regime that constrains and oppresses. Galatians 4:24 speaks of the covenant of Sinai "giving birth to servitude," and Galatians 5:1 exhorts believers not to fall back "under the yoke of servitude."
G1397.origine: The word δουλεία comes from the verb δουλεύω (to serve, to be a slave) and the noun δοῦλος (slave, servant). In Hebrew, it corresponds to עֶבֶד (servitude, slavery), with the fundamental idea of a person enslaved to another. The root evokes the bond of complete dependence: one who is in servitude no longer belongs to themselves, but to their master.
G1397.emploi: The word δουλεία appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in the letters to the Romans, Galatians, and Hebrews — letters that deal with freedom in Christ. In Romans 8, Paul contrasts servitude with adoption: the believer has not received a "spirit of servitude" but the Spirit of sonship. In Romans 8:21, creation itself will be "set free from the bondage of corruption." Galatians uses this word to describe legal bondage: the covenant of Sinai "gives birth to servitude," and Paul calls to stand firm in the freedom won in Christ, without falling back "under the yoke of servitude." Hebrews 2:15 speaks of emotional slavery: those held by the fear of death. Everywhere, the word describes a condition of oppression or subjection from which Christ liberates.
G1397.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that freedom in Christ is very real and that it goes beyond the mere absence of legal constraint. Servitude can be external (slavery in the literal sense), but also internal: fear, guilt, subjection to rules that do not save. Understanding that Christ has freed us from servitude means grasping that the Christian life is not a new yoke, but a walk in sonship and freedom. For the believer, this word reminds us that we are no longer enslaved — neither to fear, nor to sin, nor to legalistic observance.

sens: to be a slave, to be subject to someone
to obey someone, to submit to their authority
to dedicate one's activity to the service of someone or something
to be under the control or domination of something abstract
G1398.detail:
1. To be a slave means to belong to a master and do what he commands. This is the basic idea of the word. When Jesus says, "No one can serve two masters" (Matthew 6:24), he speaks of complete subjection: one obeys the one whom one serves. The Pharisees object to Jesus that they have never been slaves to anyone (John 8:33), as if being free were the normal condition.

2. To serve also means to obey someone with respect and acceptance of their authority. This is what the Galatians did under the Law (Galatians 4:25): they submitted to its requirements, like a slave to his master.

3. The word can also describe a voluntary devotion: dedicating all one's strength to the service of someone, like Paul who "serves" the Lord and his brothers (Acts 20:19, Philippians 2:22). This is no longer a constraint, but a commitment of the heart.

4. Finally, to serve can mean to be dominated by something: to be a slave to sin (Romans 6:6) means to be imprisoned by it, unable to free oneself. This is the same subjection as under a tyrannical master.
G1398.origine: The word comes from "doulos" (slave) and literally means "to be a slave." It describes the action, the state of a person who belongs to a master. In Hebrew, the equivalent word is "abad" (עָבַד), which is used to translate both the service of men and the worship of God. This root evokes the idea of bending, of bowing under an authority.
G1398.emploi: The verb "to serve" appears 23 times in the New Testament. It primarily describes a relationship of complete submission to someone: serving God, serving Christ, serving the Lord (Romans 12:11, Colossians 3:24). But it also applies to servitude to sin, the Law, or the elements of the world, described as tyrannical masters from which one cannot escape (Romans 6:6, Galatians 4:8-9). Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16:13 show that the verb carries the idea of an exclusive alliance: one cannot serve two masters at the same time; one excludes the other. That is why serving Christ requires a total choice, incompatible with the servitude of sin or wealth.
G1398.portee: This word reminds the Christian that there is a servitude from which he must be freed (that of sin and the world) and another to which he can voluntarily give himself (that of Christ and righteousness). The believer's life is a transition: he cannot remain a slave to sin; he must choose whom he will serve. Paradoxically, servitude to Christ is true freedom, as it liberates from the tyranny of sin.
